But when the TypeScript compiler generates .d.ts files it includes TSDoc comments alongside the type information — so whenever you use a package with TypeScript types you also get its TSDoc comments, which your editor can turn into contextual information. Write good TSDoc for your package’s API, and your users will thank you.

Note You can validate your TSDoc comment syntax with the eslint-plugin-tsdoc package.

5.6 Summary

  1. Writing sophisticated code hinges on learning JavaScript as a functional language.
  2. Functions are first-class objects, treated just like any other object: created via literals, assigned to variables or properties, passed as parameters, returned as results, and given properties and methods.
  3. There are different types of functions — most notably function declarations, function expressions and arrow functions. Declarations must have a name and must be separate statements.
  4. Callback functions are functions other code later “calls back”, and are heavily used, especially with event handling.
  5. The versatility of functions opens up interesting possibilities: adding them to collections including arrays and sets, attaching properties for debugging tools, and wrapping them with memoization for caching.
  6. A parameter is a variable listed in a function definition, whereas an argument is a value passed at invocation.
  7. Parameter and argument lists can differ in length: unassigned parameters evaluate as undefined, and extra arguments aren’t bound to parameter names.
  8. Rest parameters let us reference remaining arguments without matching parameter names; default parameters specify values used when none is supplied.
  9. TypeScript lets you specify types and validate calls before the code runs. Return types are optional but catch bugs, and functions can be overloaded with multiple type signatures.
  10. TSDoc provides a standard format for documenting arguments and return values, and the compiler bundles those comments with type information for anyone consuming your code.

Source

Chapter 5, “First-class functions for the novice: definitions and arguments”, of Secrets of the JavaScript Ninja, Third Edition (MEAP V10) — Manning Publications. Printed pages 77–114 of the PDF edition in this repository.

All six figures (5.1–5.6) and all eighteen listings (5.1–5.18) of the chapter are included above. Figures are embedded as data URIs with the book’s captions; the #A–#E callouts are kept as annotation keys beneath each snippet.

Chapter 6

Functions for the journeyman: understanding function invocation

This chapter covers

  • An implicit function parameter: this
  • Ways of invoking functions
  • Constructors

In the previous chapter you saw that JavaScript has significant functionally oriented characteristics: we explored the difference between function call arguments and function parameters, and how values are transferred from one to the other.

This chapter introduces the oft-misunderstood this keyword, which can be thought of as an implicit function parameter. Rather than having a fixed value for a given function, this varies based on how the function is called. We’ll look at different ways of calling functions — including call and apply — and how they affect this; at how new invokes a function as a constructor; at how functions can be bound to a particular value of this; and at how arrow functions sidestep this entirely.

Do you know?

  • Why is the this parameter known as the function context?
  • What’s the difference between a function and a method?
  • What would happen if a constructor function explicitly returned an object?

The arguments parameter

Previous editions covered another implicit function argument: arguments, an array-like object containing all arguments passed to the function. Before ES2015 it was essential, being the only way to handle an arbitrary number of arguments. After ES2015 introduced rest parameters (chapter 5), its use fell out of fashion, so this book doesn’t use it.

If you’re curious, read up on it at MDN.

6.1 The this parameter: introducing the function context

When a function is invoked, in addition to the parameters representing the explicit arguments in the call, an implicit parameter named this is passed to the function. It refers to an object associated with the invocation, which is why it’s often termed the function context.

Developers coming from object-oriented languages such as Java might think they understand the notion: there this usually points to an instance of the class in which the method is defined — a common use case in modern JavaScript too:

Listing 6.1 — Using this in class methodsJavaScript
class Ninja {
  #skillLevel = 0;                // #A

  train() {                        // #B
    this.#skillLevel++;            // #B
  }                                // #B

  get skillLevel() {              // #C
    return this.#skillLevel;       // #C
  }                                // #C
}

const ninja = new Ninja();
console.assert(ninja.skillLevel === 0,
  "New ninja has skill level 0");

ninja.train();
console.assert(ninja.skillLevel === 1,
  "Skill level improves with training");
#A The # prefix denotes a private property
#B A public method
#C A public getter (the get syntax defines a method invoked when accessing a property; getters and setters are covered in chapter 9)

Here this works straightforwardly, as in other languages, letting class methods reference the instance they’re called on. But beware: invoking a function as a method is only one way a function can be invoked. What this points to isn’t — as in Java or C# — defined only by how and where the function is defined; it can also be influenced by how the function is invoked.

A key difference from traditional object-oriented languages is that functions — including class methods — can be freely assigned to variables. This is a common case where intuitions about this break down, leading to runtime errors:

An unbound methodJavaScript
const ninja = new Ninja();
const trainNinja = ninja.train;
trainNinja(); // Error!

When this code runs, the train method executes but throws an error because this is undefined. (That assumes your code runs in strict mode — which it should if you use TypeScript with reasonable configuration. Without strict mode you’ll see a different, more confusing error; strict mode’s effect on this is discussed later in the chapter.)

Note The typescript-eslint rule unbound-method detects exactly this issue — it would flag assigning the method to a variable as a potential problem.

Since the dawn of JavaScript, countless developers have hit this and wondered: “All I did was assign a function to a variable. Why on Earth did that change its behaviour?” It’s important to understand that the reassignment isn’t the problem in itself. Consider this:

Reassigning onto an object works fineJavaScript
const ninja = new Ninja();
const trainCopy = ninja.train;
ninja.trainCopy = trainCopy;
ninja.trainCopy(); // Works!

TypeScript will complain if you add a method to a class instance this way, because the method isn’t part of the instance’s type. But it’s valid JavaScript, and the reassigned train function is perfectly functional. The difference is how it’s invoked.

6.2 Invoking functions

The way a function is invoked determines how the this parameter — the function context — is established. There are four ways, each with its own nuances:

  • As a standalone function — skulk()
  • As a method — ninja.skulk(), which ties the invocation to an object
  • As a constructor — new Ninja(), in which a new object is brought into being
  • Via the apply or call methods — skulk.call(ninja) or skulk.apply(ninja)
All four invocation stylesJavaScript
function skulk(name) {}
function Ninja(name) {}

skulk("Hattori");                  // #A
(function (who) {                // #A
  return who;                  // #A
})("Hattori");                   // #A

const ninja = {
  skulk: function () {},
};
ninja.skulk("Hattori");             // #B

ninja = new Ninja("Hattori");          // #C

skulk.call(ninja, "Hattori");         // #D
skulk.apply(ninja, ["Hattori"]);        // #E
#A Invoked as a function
#B Invoked as a method of ninja
#C Invoked as a constructor
#D Invoked via the call method
#E Invoked via the apply method

Note that getters and setters are always called as a method. The only way to invoke them separately from the object they’re attached to is to extract them with something like Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor, covered in chapter 9.

6.2.1 Invocation as a standalone function

When a function isn’t invoked as a method, as a constructor, or via apply/call, we say it’s invoked as a standalone function. This happens when we use () — with or without arguments — after an expression that references the function on its own. (If the function is a property of an object, the call is a method invocation.)

Standalone invocationsJavaScript
function ninja(){};             // #A
ninja();                        // #A

const samurai = function(){};   // #B
samurai();                      // #B

(function(){})()                  // #C
#A Function declaration invoked as a function
#B Function expression invoked as a function
#C Immediately invoked function expression

Typically, the value of this for a non-arrow function invoked standalone is undefined. (Arrow functions behave completely differently, as we’ll see.) There are a few exceptions:

  1. If the function has been bound to a context with bind, this matches that context regardless of how it’s invoked.
  2. If strict mode isn’t enabled, this is the global object instead of undefined.

A word on strict mode. It arrived in ECMAScript 5 (2009) to correct aspects of the language that had come to be regarded as mistakes; the behaviour of this in standalone functions is a prime example. Originally, code referencing this.someProperty in a standalone function would silently misbehave (the global someProperty is undefined) instead of failing clearly and immediately (accessing a property of undefined throws).

Fortunately strict mode has become the norm. You can ensure it by adding "use strict" at the top of a module, but you probably don’t have to: TypeScript emits the directive by default, as do popular transpilers like Babel, and ECMAScript modules run in strict mode even without it (ESM is covered in chapter 13). Thanks to strict mode, the behaviour of this in standalone calls is straightforward: undefined unless explicitly set with bind.

6.2.2 Invocation as a method

When a non-arrow function is assigned to a property of an object and invoked by referencing the function through that property, the function is invoked as a method of that object:

Method invocationJavaScript
const ninja = {};
ninja.skulk = function(){};
ninja.skulk();

When we invoke a function as a method of an object, that object becomes the function context and is available inside the function via this. The next listing illustrates the differences and similarities between invocation as a function and as a method.

Listing 6.2 — The differences between function and method invocationsJavaScript
"use strict";                        // #A

function whatsMyContext() {            // #B
  return this;                       // #B
}                                    // #B

console.assert(whatsMyContext() === undefined, "Context is undefined");

const ninja1 = {                     // #C
  getMyThis: whatsMyContext,         // #C
};                                   // #C

console.assert(ninja1.getMyThis() === ninja1, "Working with 1st ninja");
#A Enables strict mode for this module
#B Returns the function context, which we can examine from outside
#C Creates an object with whatsMyContext set as a method called getMyThis

The power of this in JavaScript is its flexibility: a function that references this can be attached to any object and then invoked as a method of that object. But there are traps worth watching out for:

  • Only functions defined with the function declaration and function expression syntax receive their attached object as this when invoked as methods. Arrow functions and bound functions follow their own rules, discussed later.
  • Only functions called with dot notation, like ninja1.getMyThis(), receive their attached object as this. Called with bracket notation, like ninja1["getMyThis"](), a function behaves as if it were called standalone.

6.2.3 Invocation as a constructor

In modern JavaScript development you’ll typically see constructors defined as part of a class:

A class constructorJavaScript
class Ninja {
  constructor(initialSkillLevel = 0) {
    this.#skillLevel = initialSkillLevel;
  }
  // other properties...
}

However constructors have been around since before the class keyword existed. In fact, any function created with the function declaration or expression syntax (but not arrow or bound functions) can be used as a constructor; the difference is in how the function is invoked. To invoke a function as a constructor we precede the invocation with the keyword new. Recall whatsMyContext from the previous section:

Invoking an ordinary function with newJavaScript
function whatsMyContext() {
  return this;
}

const whatsMyContextInstance = new whatsMyContext();
console.assert(whatsMyContextInstance instanceof newWhatsMyContext);

Even though we can invoke it as a constructor, whatsMyContext isn’t a particularly useful constructor. To see why, consider what makes constructors special.

The superpowers of constructors

Invoking a function as a constructor is a powerful feature, explored in the following listing.

Listing 6.3 — Using an ordinary function as a constructorJavaScript
function Ninja() {                    // #A
  this.skulk = function () {       // #A
    return this;                    // #A
  };                                 // #A
}                                    // #A

const ninja1 = new Ninja();          // #B
const ninja2 = new Ninja();          // #B

console.assert(ninja1.skulk() === ninja1,
  "The 1st ninja is skulking");        // #C
console.assert(ninja2.skulk() === ninja2,
  "The 2nd ninja is skulking");        // #C
#A A constructor that creates a skulk property on whatever object is the function context. It’s conventional to capitalise constructor names.
#B Creates two objects by invoking the constructor with new; the new objects are referenced by ninja1 and ninja2
#C Tests the skulk method of the constructed objects — each should return its own constructed object

We create a function named Ninja to construct, well, ninjas. Invoked with new, an empty object instance is created and passed to the function as its function context, this. The constructor creates a skulk property on that object, assigned a function, making it a method of the newly created object.

In general, invoking a constructor triggers a couple of special actions, as figure 6.1 shows:

  1. A new empty object is created.
  2. That object is passed to the constructor as the this parameter, becoming the constructor’s function context.
  3. The newly constructed object is returned as the new operator’s value — unless another non-primitive value is explicitly returned.

That’s it: calling a function with new returns the this object — as long as the function doesn’t explicitly return a different object.

Using explicit returns in a constructor function

JavaScript behaves counterintuitively when a function invoked with new uses return:

  • If the value after return is an object (anything other than a primitive), that value is returned from the constructor instead of this.
  • If the value after return is a primitive, the would-be return value is ignored and this is returned instead.

As a rule, avoid explicit returns in constructors. If you must use one, define a “construct signature” to tell the type checker what you actually want the function to return when invoked with new — see the TypeScript handbook.

Note ESLint’s recommended ruleset includes several rules related to constructors, including a lifesaver called no-new-native-nonconstructor that prevents you from using new with built-in functions like Symbol that aren’t intended to be called as constructors, despite their capitalisation.

Checking if a function was called as a constructor

The fact that any function can be called as a constructor (but most shouldn’t!) is one of the language’s quirks, thankfully smoothed over by improved tooling — particularly TypeScript and ESLint. It used to be common for libraries to let functions be invoked with or without new; remnants of that flexible attitude survive in built-ins: 

const obj1 = new Object();
const obj2 = Object(); // equivalent to new Object()

Originally the best check was this instanceof func, but that wasn’t completely reliable since there are other ways for the caller to make this an instance of func. ES2015 introduced new.target, which works as a fool-proof check: 

function maybeConstructor() {
  if (new.target !== undefined) {
    console.log("I was called with new");
  } else {
    console.log("I was called without new");
  }
}

Typically you should define constructors as part of a class: among other advantages, that makes the question “Am I a constructor?” moot (classes are covered in chapter 9). Outside classes, generally avoid new, and stick to capitalising class names — not normal function names — to keep the two clearly differentiated.

6.2.4 Invocation with the apply and call methods

So far you’ve seen different types of invocation implicitly change this: for methods the owning object, for top-level functions undefined (in strict mode), for constructors a newly created instance. But what if we want to set the function context explicitly? Two methods that exist for every function do exactly that: apply and call.

Yes — methods of functions. As first-class objects (created, by the way, by the built-in Function constructor), functions can have properties just like any other object type, including methods.

To invoke a function through apply, pass two parameters: the object to use as the function context, and an array of values to use as invocation arguments. call works similarly, except the arguments are passed directly in the argument list rather than as an array.

Listing 6.4 — Using the apply and call methods to supply the function contextTypeScript
function juggle(...numbers: number[]) {   // #A
  let result = 0;                            // #A
  for (const number of numbers) {           // #A
    result += number;                          // #A
  }                                            // #A
  this.result = result;                        // #A
}                                              // #A

const ninja1 = { result: 0 };
const ninja2 = { result: 0 };

juggle.apply(ninja1, [1, 2, 3, 4]);       // #B
juggle.call(ninja2, 5, 6, 7, 8);          // #C

console.assert(ninja1.result === 10, "juggled via apply");
console.assert(ninja2.result === 26, "juggled via call");
#A The function attaches the sum of its arguments to whatever object is the function context
#B Uses the apply method, passing ninja1 and an array of arguments
#C Uses the call method, passing ninja2 and a list of arguments

Here we set up a function named juggle and used it as if it were a method of ninja1 and ninja2, without actually attaching it to those objects. That’s the power of apply and call! The only difference between them is how arguments are supplied — an array for apply, a list after the function context for call. See figure 6.2.

In the early days of JavaScript, the ability to pass an array of arguments to a function with apply was invaluable — you’d often see it where this was irrelevant:

apply in its classic roleJavaScript
const numbers = [3, 7, 2];
Math.max.apply(null, numbers); // 7

Today the spread operator (chapter 5) gives a more straightforward syntax for using an array as an argument list:

The modern equivalentJavaScript
const numbers = [3, 7, 2];
Math.max(...numbers); // 7

Modern features like the spread operator and bind have made call and apply much less common. But if you ever want to “borrow” a method from one object for another, they’re the solution.

6.3 Fixing the problem of function contexts

The value of this changes depending on how a function is invoked — which can be a big problem when someone else is invoking your function. A common mistake is passing a method as a callback argument and expecting it to be invoked as a method. To demonstrate, let’s modify the DOM event list example from chapter 3.

Listing 6.5 — Passing an unbound method to an event handlerHTML
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <title>Web App Lifecycle</title>
  <style>
    #event-list li {
      font: 1.25rem system-ui;
      padding: 0.25rem 0;
    }
  </style>
</head>
<body>
  <button id="button">Click Me!</button>
  <ul id="event-list"></ul>
  <script>
    const eventList = document.querySelector("#event-list");

    const appendToEventList = (message) => {
      const messageElement = document.createElement("li");
      messageElement.textContent = message;
      eventList.appendChild(messageElement);
    };

    const buttonObject = {
      clickCount: 0,
      clickHandler: function () {
        this.clickCount++;
        appendToEventList(`Click count: ${this.clickCount}`);
      },
    };

    const buttonElement = document.getElementById("button");
    buttonElement.addEventListener(
      "click",
      buttonObject.clickHandler   // unbound method
    );
  </script>
</body>
</html>

If you click the button you’ll see that this.clickCount isn’t a number, because this isn’t buttonObject:

file:///…/index.html
  • Click count: NaN
  • Click count: NaN
  • Click count: NaN

When you pass buttonObject.clickHandler to a function, that function merely receives clickHandler. It has no way of knowing what object it was attached to. We call this an unbound method.

Fortunately modern JavaScript has two elegant tools for the problem: function binding and arrow functions.

6.3.1 Using the bind method

You’ve already met call and apply; every function also offers bind. Rather than invoking the function, bind creates a new function with the same body, but whose context is always bound to a certain object regardless of how we invoke it. To demonstrate, let’s modify listing 6.5:

Binding the handlerJavaScript
buttonElement.addEventListener(
  "click",
  buttonObject.clickHandler.bind(buttonObject), // #A
);
#A Creates a copy of clickHandler that’s bound to buttonObject

Because we pass the handler a copy of clickHandler bound to buttonObject, clicking the button now produces the output we want:

file:///…/index.html
  • Click count: 1
  • Click count: 2
  • Click count: 3

In a bound function, this is always the object it was bound to, regardless of how the bound function is invoked. Otherwise the bound function behaves like the original, since the body is the same.

It’s worth emphasising that bind creates a new function every time it’s called, without modifying the function it was called on. It’s a common mistake to expect it to “bind” the existing function in place.

Binding became so useful that for a while it was common for class constructors to replace every method with a bound copy. Fortunately ES2022 introduced a convenient syntax for defining bound methods on classes:

A bound class fieldJavaScript
class Button {
  #clickCount = 0;
  clickHandler = () => {
    this.#clickCount++;
    appendToEventList(`Click count: ${this.clickCount}`);
  }
}

Notice the use of = instead of : after the function name — strange, isn’t it? Functions defined this way are class fields, covered in depth in chapter 9. Class fields are technically a special kind of arrow function, so next we look at arrow functions generally and how they interact with this completely differently from other functions.

6.3.2 Using arrow functions to get around function contexts

Chapter 5 showed how to define arrow functions, but not the problem they were designed to solve: that problem is callbacks. The ability to pass functions around freely is one of JavaScript’s most powerful features, but there were two points of friction — the verbose function() {} syntax, and the often counterintuitive behaviour of this. Arrow functions delivered both a more succinct syntax and a straightforward solution: lexical context. The value of this inside an arrow function is simply whatever the value of this is outside it, regardless of how the function is invoked.

To understand lexical context, go back to the constructor example in listing 6.3. Before arrow functions, developers often used this pattern in constructors to avoid this entirely:

The pre-arrow workaroundJavaScript
function Ninja() {
  const _this = this;
  this.skulk = function () {
    return _this;
  };
}

With that change, calling skulk from an instance of Ninja always returns that instance, regardless of how it’s invoked — because it isn’t using its own this, it’s using this from the surrounding function context. And that’s exactly what arrow functions do:

Lexical thisJavaScript
function Ninja() {
  this.skulk = () => {
    return this;
  };
}

Because skulk is an arrow function, this comes from its lexical context — the instance of Ninja it was attached to. And that behaviour is guaranteed: even the techniques for directly controlling this have no effect.

  • Calling an arrow function with call or apply invokes it but doesn’t affect this.
  • Copying an arrow function with bind creates a copy with the same this as the original.

This is quite powerful, and as a bonus it means TypeScript can reliably predict the type of this in arrow functions — which can save you a lot of trouble.

Just remember that ordinary objects don’t create a lexical context; only functions (and, as of ES2022, classes) do. Looking at listing 6.5 again, it might be tempting to do this:

Don’t do thisJavaScript
const buttonObject = {
  clickCount: 0,
  clickHandler: () => { // don’t do this!
    this.clickCount++;
    appendToEventList(`Click count: ${this.clickCount}`);
  },
};

The value of this when defining clickHandler there is whatever it is in the surrounding function. Unlike with class fields, there’s no way to directly define a bound method on a normal JavaScript object.

Instead, the common way to use arrow functions here is to wrap the entire method invocation in one:

Wrapping the callJavaScript
buttonElement.addEventListener(
  "click",
  () => { buttonObject.clickHandler(); }, // #A
);
#A An arrow function used as the event handler

This solution doesn’t take advantage of the arrow function’s special handling of this — a plain function expression would work just as well as the wrapper — but the succinctness makes it very common. Just be careful to pass through any arguments you want; when in doubt, use rest parameters:

Passing arguments throughJavaScript
(...args) => { buttonObject.clickHandler(...args); }

And with that we’ve finished exploring function context. The next chapter deals with one of the most important concepts in JavaScript: closures.

6.4 Summary

  1. The this keyword is an implicit function parameter representing the context in which a function was invoked. How it’s determined can depend both on how a function is defined and on how it’s invoked.
  2. Arrow functions always have the same this as their surrounding context, regardless of how they’re invoked.
  3. Class fields are a special type of arrow function that is permanently bound to a class instance.
  4. A function can be invoked in four ways: standalone (skulk()), as a method (ninja.skulk()), as a constructor (new Ninja()), or via apply/call (skulk.call(ninja), skulk.apply(ninja)).
  5. The way a function is invoked influences this: standalone gives undefined (in strict mode); a method gives the object it was invoked on; a constructor gives the newly constructed object; call/apply give the first argument supplied.
  6. bind creates a new function always bound to its argument — unless the function is an arrow function, in which case the new function is identical to the original in every way.

Source

Chapter 6, “Functions for the journeyman: understanding function invocation”, of Secrets of the JavaScript Ninja, Third Edition (MEAP V10) — Manning Publications. Printed pages 115–134 of the PDF edition in this repository.

Both figures (6.1, 6.2) and all five listings (6.1–6.5) are included above, with the book’s #A–#C callouts kept as annotation keys beneath each snippet.

Chapter 7

Functions for the master: closures and scopes

This chapter covers

  • Exploring how closures work
  • How variables are scoped
  • When hoisting occurs

Closely tied to the functions we learned about in previous chapters, closures are a defining feature of JavaScript. Although many JavaScript developers write code without understanding exactly how closures work, their use is essential to many common JavaScript patterns. For example, any tasks involving callbacks, such as event handling or animations, would be significantly more complex without closures.

Closures are a side effect of how scopes work in JavaScript. For that reason, this chapter will explore the scoping rules of JavaScript. Understanding scopes will allow you to take full advantage of closures. Let’s jump right in!

Do you know?

  • How can callback functions cause memory leaks?
  • When does JavaScript create a new scope?
  • Why can some functions be referenced before they’re defined?

7.1 Understanding closures

A closure allows a function to access and manipulate variables that are external to that function. Closures allow a function to access all the variables, as well as other functions, that are in scope when the function itself is defined.

Note A scope refers to the visibility of identifiers in certain parts of a program. A scope is a part of the program in which a certain name is bound to a certain variable.

That may seem intuitive until you remember that a declared function can be called at any later time, even after the scope in which it was declared has gone away. That kind of reference simply isn’t possible in traditional imperative languages like C.

This concept is probably best explained through code:

Listing 7.1 — A simple closureJavaScript
const outerValue = "ninja";              // #A
const outerFunction = () => {          // #B
  console.assert(outerValue === "ninja", "I see the ninja.");
};

outerFunction();
#A Defines a value in module scope
#B Declares a function in the same scope as the value

In this code example, we declare a variable outerValue and a function outerFunction in the same scope. Afterward, we call outerFunction. The function is able to “see” the outerValue variable.

That might not seem so impressive. But consider what happens if you export the function and later call it from another module: the assertion would still pass. Even though the module has finished execution, the scope is still “live,” and will be for as long as any reference to outerFunction exists.

Let’s look at how this concept extends to nested scopes:

Listing 7.2 — Another closure exampleJavaScript
const outerValue = "samurai";
let func = () => {
  console.assert(false, "The original func should never be called.");
};

const outerFunction = () => {
  const innerValue = "ninja";              // #A
  const innerFunction = () => {             // #B
    console.assert(outerValue === "samurai", "I see the samurai.");
    console.assert(innerValue === "ninja", "I see the ninja.");
  };
  func = innerFunction;                        // #C
};

outerFunction();
func();
#A Declares a value within the outerFunction scope
#B Declares a function within the outerFunction scope
#C Stores a reference to innerFunction in the variable func, which was declared outside of the outerFunction scope

When we run this code, the assertions pass. That means that outerValue and innerValue are both visible to innerFunction, even when innerFunction is reassigned and invoked from a scope where innerValue doesn’t exist.

How can that be? What magic allows the innerValue variable to still be “live” when we execute the inner function, long after the scope in which it was created has gone away? The answer is closures.

When we declare innerFunction inside the outer function, not only is the function declaration defined, but a closure is created that encompasses the function definition as well as all variables in scope at the point of function definition. When innerFunction eventually executes, even if it’s executed after the scope in which it was declared goes away, it has access to the original scope in which it was declared through its closure, as shown in figure 7.1.

That’s what closures are all about. They create a “bubble” containing the function and all of the variables in scope from the function, so that the function has all it needs to execute. This bubble stays around as long as the function does. In technical terms, the closure prevents the JavaScript engine from garbage-collecting the variables in scope until the function itself is garbage-collected. We’ll look at the downsides of that garbage-collection behavior in section 7.5.

Now that you understand closures as a concept, let’s look at their practical uses.

7.2 Putting closures to work

Now that we have a high-level understanding of closures, let’s see how to put them to work in our JavaScript applications. For now, we’ll focus on their practical aspects and benefits. Later in the chapter, we’ll revisit the same examples to see exactly what’s going on behind the scenes.

7.2.1 Saving values in function-scoped variables

Back in chapter 5, we introduced this memoization function, which is a great example of a common closure pattern:

The memoize function, revisitedJavaScript
function memoize(func) {
  const cache = new Map();
  return (arg) => {
    if (!cache.has(arg)) {
      cache.set(arg, func(arg));
    }
    return cache.get(arg);
  };
}

// Memoize functions with expensive computations:
const memoizedIsPrime = memoize(isPrime);

Every time memoize is called, it creates a new cache which, thanks to its scope, is only usable from the function returned by memoize. The cache will remain in memory as long as there are any live references to that function.

Back in the early days of JavaScript, this was touted to developers coming from object-oriented languages like C++ and Java as the best way to approximate the “private variables” those developers were used to. Since then, JavaScript has added a syntax for private variables in classes, as we’ll see in chapter 9. But using function scope to control access to variables remains common and useful.

7.2.2 Referencing surrounding variables from callbacks

Another common use of closures occurs when dealing with callbacks — when a function is called at an unspecified later time. Often, within such functions, we frequently need to access outside data. The following listing shows an example that creates a simple animation with callback timers.

Listing 7.3 — Using a closure in a timer interval callbackJavaScript
let tick = 0;
const timerId = setInterval(() => {          // #A
  tick++;
  console.log(`tick ${tick}`);
  if (tick === 5) {                       // #B
    clearInterval(timerId);                // #B
  }                                      // #B
}, 10);
#A Sets up a timer to call the given callback every 10 milliseconds
#B Turns off the timer once the callback has been called 5 times
tick 1
tick 2
tick 3
tick 4
tick 5

This code will run the callback 5 times. Here, the callback can see not only the tick variable that was defined before the callback, but also the timerId variable that was defined in the same line as the callback. It might be surprising that JavaScript allows that, but functions are allowed to reference anything in their lexical scope — even variables that are declared after the function. We’ll discuss the rules around this more in the next section. For now, the important thing to note is that we’re allowed to reference timerId as long as it’s initialized (assigned a value) before we do so.

Closures are closely related to scopes, so we’ll spend the rest of this chapter exploring scoping rules in JavaScript.

7.3 Variable scope and hoisting

In this section, we’ll drill down on exactly what defines a scope in JavaScript. We’ll also take a brief look at the oft-misunderstood concept of “hoisting,” where JavaScript allows certain entities to be referenced before they’re declared.

7.3.1 Creating block scopes

In all of the examples in this chapter so far, we’ve used function bodies to create new scopes. And indeed, a function body always creates a scope. But functions aren’t the only way to create a scope in JavaScript:

  • A module always creates its own scope.
  • Constructs like for, if, and switch create their own scope.
  • Curly brackets can be used on their own to create scope, a pattern known as a standalone block.

Note The var keyword plays by its own rules: it’s scoped to the nearest function (or module), ignoring other blocks. However, var is considered something of a legacy keyword. Most modern JavaScript developers prefer to consistently use const and let instead. For that reason, none of the code examples in this book use var. You can enforce that convention with ESLint’s no-var rule.

As a rule of thumb, you can determine a variable’s scope by looking for the closest pair of curly brackets, excluding the curly brackets used in the object literal syntax. A notable exception is variables declared in a for loop’s initialization, as we’ll demonstrate shortly.

This example shows several nested scopes in action:

Listing 7.4 — Nested block scopesJavaScript
const moduleScope = "module";                       // #A
{
  const standaloneBlockScope = "standalone";         // #B
  for (let loopScope = 0; loopScope < 3; loopScope++) {  // #C
    switch (loopScope) {
      case 0:
        console.log(moduleScope);
        break;
      case 1:
        console.log(standaloneBlockScope);
        break;
      case 2: {
        const caseBlockScope = "case";              // #D
        console.log(caseBlockScope);
      }
    }
  }
}
#A Declares a variable in the scope of the module
#B Declares a variable in the scope of the standalone block
#C Declares a variable in the scope of the for loop
#D Declares a variable in the scope of the case block

Each variable here has its own scope. Aside from the module scope, each of these is called a block scope because it’s delimited as a “block” by curly brackets (with the exception of the for loop, where the initializer is considered to be part of the same block as the loop body).

It’s worth highlighting a feature of for loop block scope: each iteration of the loop is considered a new block, which means that closures that reference any values in the loop scope will reference those values as of the loop iteration the closure was created in.

Listing 7.5 — Loop scope and closuresJavaScript
for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  setTimeout(() => {
    console.log(i);
  }, 10);
}
0
1
2

Each iteration of this loop sets up a timer, and those timers won’t go off until after the loop has finished iterating. So you might expect the final value of i to be emitted three times. And indeed, that would be the behavior if the loop variable were declared with var i, scoping it to the closest function or module. But because we used let i, each timer callback sees the value of i from the loop iteration it was declared in.

This more-intuitive loop behavior is one of the major advantages of let over var!

Now you know how to create scopes without creating functions. Next, we’ll take a look at a question that’s closely related to scope: what happens when we reference a variable or function that comes later in our code?

7.3.2 Execution order and hoisting

Just because a variable is in scope doesn’t mean you can reference it. Consider this code:

Referencing a block-scoped variable too earlyJavaScript
console.assert(x === 1, "x is 1");
const x = 1;

The reference to x is executed before x is initialized. If you type check the code with TypeScript, it’ll describe the problem this way: 

Block-scoped variable 'x' used before its declaration.

If you were to ignore that warning and run the code anyway, you’d get a runtime error:

ReferenceError: Cannot access 'x' before initialization

Note the specificity of the error message. If not for the later const x = 1 declaration on the second line, the first line would trigger this error instead: 

ReferenceError: x is not defined

This highlights a key fact about how JavaScript runs: all code in a scope is parsed to determine which variables are in that scope before execution begins. We’ll examine this behavior in more detail in section 7.3.3.

Lost in the temporal dead zone

The behavior of a ReferenceError being thrown when an uninitialized variable is referenced is unique to variables defined with let, const, and class. If you reference an uninitialized variable declared with var, it’ll have the value undefined. And if you reference a function declared with function, it’ll be hoisted, as described later in this section.

To differentiate these cases, the ECMAScript spec refers to variables that are in scope but will trigger a ReferenceError if referenced as being in the Temporal Dead Zone.

To avoid the dreaded ReferenceError, we need to make sure that all variables are initialized before they’re referenced. Importantly, that’s a statement about execution order, not the order of the code itself. Consider this example:

Order of execution, not order of codeJavaScript
const verifyX = () => {
  console.assert(x === 1, "x is 1");
};
const x = 1;
verifyX();

This code runs perfectly fine with no errors. The fact that the body of the verifyX function references x before it’s defined is irrelevant; what matters is that the function is executed after x is defined.

Note TypeScript can’t determine whether a function is called before or after all of the variables referenced from that function are defined. To avoid potential runtime errors, you can use ESLint’s no-use-before-define rule to ensure that variables are always defined before they’re used.

Where things get interesting is function declarations. As you’ll recall from chapter 5, a function declaration refers specifically to a function that’s defined with the syntax function functionName( /* parameters */ ) { /* function body */ }. Function declarations have the special property that they’re always treated as if they were declared at the top of the scope, meaning that they can be referenced from anywhere within the same scope. This feature is known as hoisting:

Listing 7.6 — Accessing a function before its declarationJavaScript
greetNinja();
function greetNinja() {
  console.log(getGreeting());
}
function getGreeting() {
  return "Ossu!";
}
Ossu!

If you run this code, you’ll get the output above. Hoisting defies our intuitive expectations of execution order. When the greetNinja() call runs, none of the code after that line has been executed. And yet, not only is the reference to the function resolved successfully, but that function is also able to reference an even later function.

It’s worth emphasizing: functions defined with any other syntax don’t have this strange behavior! Only function declarations do. Aside from function declarations, the only other constructs that get hoisted in JavaScript (assuming that strict mode is enabled) are imports defined with the import keyword. We’ll learn about imports in chapter 13.

Before we move on, let’s take a peek under the hood and learn how JavaScript engines implement these scoping rules.

7.3.3 Parsing and scope analysis

As we’ve seen, the JavaScript engine “knows” that a variable is in scope even before the declaration for that variable runs. It’s able to pull off this magic trick by parsing the code and constructing scopes before execution begins. In fact, modern JavaScript engines generally perform parsing in two separate passes:

  1. Syntax validation to identify syntax errors.
  2. Full parsing where the engine compiles the code to bytecode.

Note Modern JavaScript engines are extremely complex. The description here is a simplified model that may not always apply. For instance, an engine may sometimes combine syntax validation and full parsing in a single pass as an optimization. If you want to dive deep and learn more about how JavaScript engines actually work, the site for Google’s V8 has a number of articles detailing its inner workings.

The syntax validation pass runs over all code. Consider this example:

A syntax error, found before anything runsJavaScript
console.log("func is not defined yet.");
const func = () => {
  let a = 1;
  const a = 2;
};

Using the same identifier for a variable in the exact same scope is considered a syntax error in JavaScript, just as a mismatched curly bracket would be. Trying to run the example above yields this error: 

SyntaxError: Identifier 'a' has already been declared

The console.log at the top of the script never runs, because syntax validation occurs before code execution. Performing syntax validation up-front like this is mandated by the ECMAScript spec.

That fact has a major implication for performance: as JavaScript programs get larger, they’ll necessarily take more time to start up, as the engine has to scan through all of its code looking for syntax errors before execution can begin. (This can be solved with lazy loading, which we’ll look at in chapter 13.) Fortunately, syntax validation is much faster than full parsing.

It’s during the full parsing pass that the engine constructs scopes, a process called scope analysis. As we’ve seen, scope analysis precedes code execution. Crucially, though, the JavaScript engine can wait until code execution begins in a particular scope to perform scope analysis.

This, too, has a major implication for performance: in order to start code execution as quickly as possible, JavaScript engines will often defer full parsing, an optimization known as lazy parsing. In practice, the best candidates for lazy parsing are large functions. Consider a complex JavaScript CLI program:

Everything parsed up-frontTypeScript
import * as readlinePromises from "node:readline/promises";
import { stdin, stdout } from "node:process";

const rl = readlinePromises.createInterface({
  input: stdin,
  output: stdout,
});

while (true) {
  const input = await rl.question('Enter command or ".exit":\n> ');
  switch (input) {
    case ".exit":
      process.exit(0);
    // Handlers for hundreds of other commands...
  }
}

As the switch statement grows, so too will the program’s startup time. The JavaScript engine will not only scan the program for syntax errors, but also fully parse all of the code. Now consider what happens if we move that complex logic into a function:

The same program, with the big switch in a functionTypeScript
import * as readlinePromises from "node:readline/promises";
import { stdin, stdout } from "node:process";

const handleInput = (input: string) => {
  switch (input) {
    case ".exit":
      process.exit(0);
    // Handlers for hundreds of other cases...
  }
};

const rl = readlinePromises.createInterface({
  input: stdin,
  output: stdout,
});

while (true) {
  const input = await rl.question('Enter command or ".exit":\n> ');
  handleInput(input);
}

Now the JavaScript engine only needs to scan the program for syntax errors and fully parse the outer scope before execution can begin, which means that the user will get the prompt faster. And modern JavaScript engines perform background compilation while the event loop is idle, which means that at least some of the work of fully parsing the handleInput function would likely be completed before the user enters their first command.

Note Google’s Lighthouse tool offers a breakdown of the time spent running JavaScript on a web page, with parse time shown separately from evaluation time: bootup time.

In the next section, we’ll look at one very special JavaScript scope.

7.4 The global scope object

Back in the early days of JavaScript, declaring global variables was easy. Too easy. There were no modules; if you wanted a non-global scope, you had to wrap your code in a function. And even then, you could easily create a global variable by accident:

The old accidental-global trickJavaScript
(function localScope() {
  ninjaName = "Naruto";
  // other code...
})();

console.assert(ninjaName === "Naruto", "ninjaName is global");

Without the var keyword (or, starting in ES5, const and let), assigning a value to an unrecognized variable name would simply create a global variable with that name. Worse, assigning a variable to an existing global variable name would overwrite that variable (if that global was overwritable)!

Thankfully, as JavaScript has modernized, the problem of accidental globals has largely faded away. Code is typically written in modules, in which the top-level scope is the module’s scope, not the global scope. And as long as strict mode is enabled, assigning a value to a variable that hasn’t been declared is illegal:

Strict mode rejects accidental globalsJavaScript
"use strict";
ninjaName = "Naruto"; // ReferenceError: ninjaName is not defined

But what if you do want to define a variable globally, so that even code in other modules can access it without importing it? No problem: just attach it to the global object.

Listing 7.7 — Attaching a value to the global objectTypeScript
// In globals.mts
declare global {                           // #A
  var ninjaName: string;               // #A
}                                        // #A
globalThis.ninjaName = "Naruto";            // #B

// In main.mts
import "./globals.mts";                    // #C
console.log(`It's me, ${ninjaName}!`);
#A A TypeScript construct that tells the type checker that we’re defining a global variable
#B Attaches a value to the ninjaName property of the global object, globalThis
#C Imports our globals module, executing its code

Running main.mts emits this output:

It's me, Naruto!

Before the globalThis.ninjaName line was executed, trying to reference ninjaName would’ve caused a ReferenceError. After it’s executed, ninjaName can be referenced from anywhere in the program, either as ninjaName by itself or as globalThis.ninjaName. Needless to say, the global object is a very special object!

A fun feature of the global object is that, since it’s a global variable, it can be referenced as a property of itself:

The global object contains itselfJavaScript
console.assert(globalThis.globalThis === globalThis)

The globalThis identifier is relatively new, having been introduced as part of ECMAScript 2020. Back when JavaScript was confined to the web browser, you could always expect the global object to be named window. Then Node.js came along and gave its global object the name global. That was a sensible name, but it made it tedious and error-prone to deal with globals in code that might run in either a browser or a standalone runtime. globalThis solves that problem: it’s a cross-environment standard for referencing the global object. In the browser, globalThis === window, and in Node.js, globalThis === global.

Note In today’s world where the lines are blurred between different JavaScript environments, it’s a good idea to prefer globalThis over other global object names, except when referencing environment-specific APIs like window.addEventListener. The eslint-plugin-unicorn package offers a prefer-global-this rule to enforce that preference.

Let’s put everything we know about scopes together. Whenever you reference a variable, the JavaScript engine resolves it by traversing the scope chain, which refers to all of the scopes from the local scope on up to the global scope. The algorithm goes like this, starting in the local scope:

  1. Check if the current scope has a variable with that name. If it does:
    1. If the variable is initialized (or can be hoisted), resolve to that variable.
    2. If the variable is uninitialized, throw a ReferenceError.
  2. If no match was found in the current scope:
    1. If we’re in the global scope, throw a ReferenceError.
    2. Otherwise, repeat this process in the parent scope.

Checking whether a global exists with typeof

What if you want to reference a variable that may or may not have been initialized? You could use a try/catch block to deal with the ReferenceError, but a more elegant approach is to use typeof. When you put the typeof keyword in front of an undeclared variable, you’ll get the string "undefined" instead of a ReferenceError. For example:

Guarding an optional global with typeofJavaScript
const initializeGlobalName = () => {
  if (typeof ninjaName === "undefined") {
    globalThis.ninjaName = "Naruto";
  }
}

Since the global object is an object, you could also do a check like if ("ninjaName" in globalThis). But the typeof check is generally more common.

Note that under most circumstances, checking typeof ninjaName === "undefined" is equivalent to checking ninjaName === undefined. The two checks only differ in the case where ninjaName may or may not have been declared as a global, since referencing an undeclared global without typeof would trigger a ReferenceError.

One word of caution: typeof can only be used to check whether a variable exists in the global scope. If you try to use it with a variable that’s declared in a local scope, you’ll run into the dreaded Temporal Dead Zone:

typeof can’t rescue a local variableJavaScript
console.log(typeof x); // throws ReferenceError
const x = 1;

If you really need to know whether a local variable has been initialized, your only option is the try/catch block. In practice, you should be able to avoid this situation by moving the variable declaration to the top of the scope block.

In the next section, we’ll look at one of the downsides of JavaScript’s flexible scoping rules: the potential for memory leaks.

7.5 Preventing memory leaks

JavaScript is a garbage-collected language, meaning that the runtime automatically frees up memory from objects that are no longer referenced. But what, exactly, does “no longer referenced” mean?

As we’ve seen in the preceding sections, a JavaScript function can reference all variables from its surrounding scope. Thanks to closures, that function can even reference variables defined in an outer scope that’s finished execution. The scope is kept “live” by the function that has access to that scope.

So, will the JavaScript runtime free up a specific object if that object isn’t directly referenced but its scope is still live? The answer is: sometimes! The exact garbage-collection behavior isn’t prescribed by the ECMAScript spec, so each JavaScript engine has its own set of heuristics. In a blog post, “Garbage collection and closures”, Jake Archibald gives an example of a situation where all of the major JavaScript engines keep an object alive long after it’s needed, causing a memory leak. Listing 7.8 is adapted from his example.

Note Unlike most of the code in this book, listing 7.8 must be run in one specific JavaScript runtime: Node.js. That’s because we’re hooking in to the internals of Node.js’s JavaScript engine, V8, which it exposes for debugging purposes. You can find the docs for the Node.js v8 module online.

Listing 7.8 — A closure-induced memory leakJavaScript
import { writeHeapSnapshot } from "v8";

const prepareNinjaPower = () => {
  const powerBuffer = new ArrayBuffer(99_000_000);      // #A
  (() => {                                             // #B
    console.log(`Ninja power level: ${               // #B
      powerBuffer.byteLength.toLocaleString()}`);       // #B
  })();                                                // #B
  return () => {                                       // #C
    console.log("The ninja power is safe.");       // #C
  };                                                   // #C
};

const reportNinjaPower = prepareNinjaPower();
reportNinjaPower();
writeHeapSnapshot("1-before-gc.heapsnapshot");           // #D

if (global.gc) {                                       // #E
  console.log("Running garbage collection");        // #E
  global.gc(true);                                  // #E
  writeHeapSnapshot("2-after-gc.heapsnapshot");         // #E
}                                                     // #E
#A Creates a large object. ArrayBuffer’s constructor takes a number of bytes to allocate
#B Immediately runs a function that references the ArrayBuffer
#C Returns a function that doesn’t reference the ArrayBuffer
#D Saves a heap snapshot to a file
#E Forces garbage collection to run immediately (if the API is available), then saves a second heap snapshot

If you examine the heap snapshot files, you can see that there’s an object that’s approximately 100 MB in size in both the before and after, which means that powerBuffer isn’t garbage-collected. By contrast, if you run prepareNinjaPower without assigning its return value to a variable, that 100 MB object disappears!

The problem is that (as of this writing) the V8 engine used by Node.js uses heuristic reasoning along these lines:

  1. There’s a closure that references powerBuffer.
  2. There’s a function in the same scope that lives after prepareNinjaPower runs.
  3. Therefore, powerBuffer must be kept in memory as long as that returned function is alive.

That reasoning is wrong, of course: powerBuffer isn’t needed after the IIFE runs. A lot of very smart engineers work on the V8 engine, and they’re aware of this issue. The problem is that fixing it would require the engine to manage more information about which closures reference which variables, which would reduce performance in other situations. It’s a challenging tradeoff with no easy solutions. The best thing you can do as a JavaScript Ninja is to be aware of the issue.

Note If there’s ever any doubt about whether the JavaScript engine will garbage-collect a large object, the most reliable option is to explicitly delete it when it’s no longer needed. TypeScript 5.2 introduced a using keyword, based on a proposed ECMAScript feature, that can simplify the process — see the TypeScript 5.2 release notes.

And with that, you can consider yourself a master of JavaScript’s scope rules. In the next chapter, we’ll look at promises and generators, two invaluable features for working with asynchronous code.

7.6 Summary

Six things to remember

  1. Closures are a built-in feature of all JavaScript functions that allow a function to access all variables that are in scope when the function itself was defined. They create a “safety bubble” of the function and the variables that are in scope at the point of the function’s definition. This way, the function has all it needs to execute, even if the scope in which the function was created is long gone.
  2. Any block of code with { and } defines a new scope — unless that block is an object literal.
    • Variables defined in a for loop initializer are considered to be in the same scope as the loop body, and each iteration has its own scope.
  3. The let and const keywords define a variable in the closest scope, as do keywords like function and class. The older var keyword has its own scoping rules, but most JavaScript developers prefer not to use it.
  4. A variable can’t be referenced until its declaration has been executed, with the exception of function declarations and imports, which are “hoisted” to the top of their scope.
  5. The global scope in JavaScript contains the properties of an object called globalThis. You can declare global variables by attaching them to that global object.
  6. JavaScript engines may sometimes avoid garbage-collecting variables in a scope with live closures, which can lead to memory leaks.

Source

Chapter 7, “Functions for the master: closures and scopes”, of Secrets of the JavaScript Ninja, Third Edition (MEAP V10) — Manning Publications. Printed pages 135–153 of the PDF edition in this repository.

Figure 7.1 and all eight listings (7.1–7.8) are included above, with the book’s #A–#E callouts kept as annotation keys beneath each snippet. The chapter has no second figure: the only illustration in it is the closure “bubble” of figure 7.1.

Chapter 8

Functions for the future: promises and generators

This chapter covers

  • Handling asynchronous tasks with promises
  • Using the async/await syntax instead of callbacks
  • Continuing function execution with generators

In the previous three chapters, we focused on functions, specifically on how to define functions and how to use them to great effect. In some cases, we’ve passed a function as a callback to be invoked when some event occurs in the future. Callbacks have always been a part of JavaScript and remain a common pattern. However, they aren’t the only way to deal with future events. One of the most important features in modern JavaScript is the promise, an object representation of an event.

As we’ll soon see, promises and the associated async and await keywords have become the preferred way of dealing with events in a wide variety of situations. We’ll also look at generators, a lesser-used JavaScript feature that can provide a convenient alternative to loops, both synchronous and asynchronous.

8.1 The power of promises

A promise is an object that represents the outcome of an operation. Since their introduction in ES2015, promises have become a ubiquitous part of the JavaScript language, beloved by developers for their convenience and flexibility.

Promises are often touted as an alternative to callbacks, and we’ll soon see why. But in its purest form, a promise is just a way of moving a callback. Let’s start with a simple example:

Listing 8.1 — A promise for a timerJavaScript
const timerPromise = new Promise((resolve) => {   // #A
  setTimeout(resolve, 1_000);                          // #B
});

timerPromise.then(() => {                            // #C
  console.log("One second has elapsed");
});
#A The promise constructor provides a callback function to resolve the promise
#B The timeout will invoke the resolve function after 1,000 milliseconds
#C The promise’s .then method takes a callback that’s invoked when resolve is called

Here we could have done without the promise and simply passed the callback with the console.log directly to setTimeout. But by encapsulating the event result in a promise, we’ve opened up a number of intriguing possibilities:

  • The promise can be passed around freely, allowing any code with access to the object to attach its own handler for the event.
  • There’s no limit to the number of times then can be called on the same promise; any number of callbacks can be queued up.
  • We can write utility functions that take advantage of these properties to perform higher-level operations, such as performing an action after multiple promises have been resolved.

And it gets better! ES2017 introduced two keywords, async and await, that provide a sleek syntax for common promise patterns. With the await keyword, listing 8.1 can be simplified to this:

The same timer, with awaitJavaScript
const timerPromise = new Promise((resolve) => {
  setTimeout(resolve, 1_000);
});
await timerPromise;
console.log("One second has elapsed");

At first glance, that code defies our claim that JavaScript is a single-threaded language. But make no mistake: there’s only one thread here! We’ll see how the await keyword pulls off this feat in section 8.2.

But before you can understand await, you’ll need to understand promises. Let’s examine the functionality of promises in more detail.

8.1.1 Resolving and settling promises

A promise is always in one of three states: pending, fulfilled, or rejected. The fulfilled state typically represents a successful event, while the rejected state is typically used for errors. When a promise is either fulfilled or rejected, we say that it’s settled. In addition to its state, a promise also takes an associated value when it’s settled.

Importantly, a promise’s state can only change once. Once it’s settled, its state and value are set permanently (figure 8.1).

To make this more concrete, let’s look at the complete promise constructor:

The promise constructorJavaScript
const promise = new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
  // code that calls resolve or reject eventually...
});

The constructor returns a promise that starts in the pending state and takes a callback known as the executor, which runs immediately when the promise is created. The executor gives you control over the promise’s fate through its two parameters: resolve and reject.

Importantly, the promise object itself doesn’t provide any methods for changing its state — that can only be done from within the executor. (The promise’s state can’t be read directly from the promise object either, though some developer tools are able to display it by reading it from internal APIs.) There are three ways to change the promise’s state:

  1. By calling resolve
  2. By calling reject
  3. By throwing an error from the executor

Those last two mechanisms behave straightforwardly: calling reject(reason) will make the promise rejected with the given reason, and throwing reason from the executor body will have the same effect. By convention, reason is typically an instance of Error, though this isn’t enforced. That’s consistent with the behavior of throw: JavaScript allows any value to be thrown, but it’s considered best practice to only throw Error instances.

The resolve function is a bit more complicated. If you call resolve(value) with a “normal” value, the promise will be fulfilled with that value. That’s what happened in our timer example: the line setTimeout(resolve, 1_000) resulted in resolve being called with no arguments, fulfilling the promise with the value undefined. But if you call resolve(value) with an object that has a then method, a category known as a thenable, then the promise will “subscribe” to that then method and make its output its own.

Since promises have a then method, every promise is a thenable. Which means that calling resolve(otherPromise) will make the promise that resolve function belongs to mimic otherPromise, matching its state and value. Let’s look at an example:

Listing 8.2 — Resolving promises with other promisesJavaScript
const fulfilledPromise = Promise.resolve("fulfilled");      // #A
const rejectedPromise = Promise.reject(new Error("rejected")); // #A

const promise1 = new Promise((resolve) => resolve(fulfilledPromise));
const promise2 = new Promise((resolve) => resolve(rejectedPromise));

promise1.then((value) => {                                 // #B
  console.log(`promise1 was fulfilled with value "${value}"`);   // #B
});                                                       // #B

promise2.then(undefined, (reason) => {                    // #C
  console.log(`promise2 was rejected with reason "${reason}"`);   // #C
});                                                       // #C
#A Promise.resolve and Promise.reject are convenience methods for creating a promise that’s immediately resolved or rejected with the given value
#B The first callback to promise.then only fires if the promise is fulfilled
#C The second callback to promise.then only fires if the promise is rejected

This example shows that calling resolve doesn’t necessarily fulfill a promise. In fact, it doesn’t even necessarily settle it. Consider this example where we call resolve with an object whose then method never invokes any callbacks passed to it:

Permanently pendingJavaScript
// Creates a promise that’s permanently pending.
new Promise((resolve) =>
  resolve({
    then: () => {},
  }),
);

This bears repeating, as it’s a common source of confusion: once a promise is either fulfilled or rejected, neither its state nor its associated value will ever change. That promise is settled. But a promise that’s been resolved with a thenable can remain unsettled.

Resolved vs. settled

The ECMAScript spec uses the term resolved to mean that the promise’s resolve or reject function has been called. As we’ve seen, knowing that a promise is resolved doesn’t tell us anything about its state, since a promise that’s resolved with another promise will mimic the other promise’s state. However, being resolved means that any further calls to resolve or reject will be ignored.

We’ll be using the term settled throughout this book to refer to a promise that’s in either the fulfilled or rejected state. But colloquially, you’ll often hear people use the term resolved when they really mean settled or fulfilled.

In most cases, you can think of resolve(thenable) as shorthand for thenable.then(resolve, reject). However, there’s one important distinction: if resolve and reject are callable from elsewhere, resolve(thenable) will cause those calls to silently fail, because a promise can only be resolved once.

By the way, just because resolve and reject are passed to the executor doesn’t mean they need to be called from the executor. Since the dawn of promises, developers have been using hacks like this to allow a promise to be resolved from a different part of their application:

Reaching outside the executorJavaScript
let resolvePromise;
let rejectPromise;
const promise = new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
  resolvePromise = resolve;
  rejectPromise = reject;
});

Happily, ES2024 introduced a convenient new static method for this scenario called Promise.withResolvers(). It does exactly what it says on the tin, returning a new promise along with the resolve and reject functions for that promise:

Promise.withResolversJavaScript
const { promise, resolve, reject } = Promise.withResolvers();

That technique provides a simple bridge between promises and callback-based APIs: you can create a promise that represents a call to that API by passing the promise’s resolve function as a callback.

Now you know everything there is to know about promise resolution! Next we’ll take a look at an area where the promise resolution algorithm really has a chance to shine: chaining.

8.1.2 Chaining promises with then()

We’ve seen how the then method allows you to pass onFulfilled and onRejected callbacks to a promise. But then has one more trick up its sleeve: it returns another promise. The promise returned by then is a new promise that starts in the pending state, then gets resolved according to the behavior of the onFulfilled or onRejected callback:

  • If the callback returns a value, the new promise is resolved with that value. This resolution follows the same rules we saw for the resolve function in the previous section.
  • If the callback throws an error (or anything else), the new promise is rejected with the thrown reason.

The promise resolution behavior means that returning a promise from a then callback effectively transforms the promise returned by then into a copy of the promise returned from the callback. This ability to return promises turns out to be enormously powerful, because we can use it to represent a chain of operations. Here’s a practical example using fetch:

Listing 8.3 — Using promise chaining to handle a fetch resultJavaScript
fetch("https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts/1")   // #A
  .then((response) => {                                 // #B
    if (!response.ok) {                                // #C
      throw new Error(`Status code ${response.status}`); // #D
    }
    return response.json();                             // #E
  })
  .then((json) => {                                     // #F
    console.log(json);                                  // #F
  })                                                    // #F
  .catch((reason) => {                                  // #G
    console.error(`Request failed: ${reason}`);          // #G
  })                                                    // #G
  .finally(() => {                                       // #H
    console.log("Request finished");                     // #H
  });                                                   // #H
#A Starts a GET request for the given URL and returns a promise
#B The promise is fulfilled when the head of the response has been parsed
#C The ok property is true if the response’s status code is 2xx, false otherwise
#D Throwing an error causes the promise returned by then to be rejected
#E Returns a promise representing the result of parsing the response body as JSON
#F The promise is fulfilled when the response body has been parsed as JSON
#G promise.catch(onRejected) is shorthand for promise.then(undefined, onRejected)
#H promise.finally runs whenever the promise is settled

When promises were first introduced, code like this was a revelation. It avoids the awkward syntax of nested callbacks (more on that in section 8.2), and perhaps more importantly, it greatly streamlines error handling. That single catch handler deals with potential errors from three different places:

  1. The fetch() itself (for example, if the user lost their network connection)
  2. The error we throw if response.ok is false (for example, if we get a response with a 500 status code)
  3. The response.json() operation (for example, if the response body isn’t valid JSON)

The name of the method is no coincidence: the promise catch method is intended as the async equivalent of the catch in a try/catch block, receiving all errors in a chain of operations. We’ll see a more explicit connection between the catch method and try/catch with the await keyword in section 8.2.

ES2018 extended the analogy between promises and try/catch further with the finally method, which takes a handler that runs when the promise is settled, regardless of whether it was fulfilled or rejected. Like catch, the finally method is a convenient shorthand for behavior that could be implemented with then.

Note One of the biggest frustrations developers have with promises is that, by default, errors are silently ignored. Handling only the fulfilled case and not the rejected case is an easy mistake to make! Fortunately, typescript-eslint offers a rule for this called no-floating-promises, which enforces that promise rejections are either explicitly handled or explicitly ignored.

It’s important to understand that each handler in a promise chain returns a new promise derived from the previous one. The then, catch, and finally methods can’t modify the state of the promise they’re attached to; only its resolve and reject functions can do that.

We’ve covered all of the basics of promises: how to consume them, how to resolve them, and how to chain them. Now let’s take a look at how promises simplify dealing with concurrent operations.

8.1.3 Dealing with multiple promises

We’ve seen how promise chaining can simplify the logic around serial async operations. But what about concurrent operations? For example, let’s say that we need to fetch data from multiple sources before we can render a UI. To be efficient, we should send these fetch requests concurrently, rather than waiting for each one to be completed before we send the next one.

Happily, the Promise object offers a static method called Promise.all for exactly this scenario. Promise.all takes an array of promises and returns a promise that represents their combined outcome:

  • If all of the promises in the array are fulfilled, the returned promise resolves with an array of all of their fulfilled values. The order of those values matches the order of the original promises.
  • If any one of the promises in the array is rejected, the returned promise is immediately rejected with the rejection reason.
Listing 8.4 — Using Promise.all to combine multiple promisesJavaScript
const allPostsPromise = Promise.all(            // #A
  [                                                // #B
    fetch("https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts/1"), // #B
    fetch("https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts/2"), // #B
    fetch("https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts/3"), // #B
  ].map((fetchPromise) =>                     // #C
    fetchPromise.then((response) => {          // #C
      if (!response.ok) {                      // #C
        throw new Error(`Status code ${response.status}`); // #C
      }                                        // #C
      return response.json();                   // #C
    }),                                        // #C
  ),                                             // #C
);

allPostsPromise
  .then((posts) => {                               // #D
    posts.forEach((post) => {                   // #D
      console.log(post);                          // #D
    });                                          // #D
  })                                             // #D
  .catch((reason) => {                             // #E
    console.error(`Request failed: ${reason}`);       // #E
  });                                            // #E
#A Returns a single promise representing the result of every promise in an array
#B Starts three fetch requests and stores the returned promises in an array
#C Transforms each fetch promise to either fulfill with parsed JSON or be rejected
#D Handles the case where all of the transformed fetch promises were fulfilled
#E Handles the case where any of the transformed fetch promises were rejected

True to its name, Promise.all is for all-or-nothing scenarios where any single failure makes the other events moot. In practice, this is the most common way of handling concurrent promises. However, if you need more flexibility, ES2020 added a method called Promise.allSettled. The allSettled method returns a promise that’s fulfilled after all of the given promises are settled, with an array containing their settled states and values. Of course, there’s nothing stopping you from combining the two: you could use Promise.all to show a generic error to the user as soon as one operation fails, then use Promise.allSettled to update that error message with details on every operation that failed.

There are two more built-in multi-promise operations that are worth mentioning: Promise.any and Promise.race. Like the other static methods we’ve mentioned, these methods take an array of promises and return a single promise:

  • Promise.any returns a promise that resolves with the first promise to be fulfilled. If all of the promises are rejected, the returned promise is rejected with an array of rejection reasons.
  • Promise.race returns a promise that resolves with whichever promise settles first, whether it’s fulfilled or rejected.

Promise.any is newer and lesser-used, but useful in cases where there are multiple ways to complete a task. For example, you might want to simultaneously send fetch requests to a database and a cache. If the cache request succeeds, great! If the cache request fails, that’s no problem as long as the database request doesn’t fail too.

Promise.race is commonly used to add a time limit to another promise. You can think of it as creating a race against the timer:

Listing 8.5 — Using Promise.race to enforce a timeoutJavaScript
const fetchController = new AbortController();              // #A
const fetchPromise = fetch("https://httpbin.org/delay/2", {  // #B
  signal: fetchController.signal,                            // #B
}).then((response) => {                                    // #B
  if (!response.ok) {                                      // #B
    throw new Error(`Status code ${response.status}`);     // #B
  }                                                        // #B
  return response.json();                                 // #B
});                                                        // #B

const timeoutPromise = new Promise((_, reject) =>         // #C
