  setTimeout(() => {                                     // #C
    fetchController.abort();                             // #C
    reject(new Error("Request timeout"));
  }, 1_000),                                             // #C
);                                                         // #C

Promise.race([fetchPromise, timeoutPromise])                // #D
  .then((result) => {
    console.log(result);
  })
  .catch((reason) => {
    console.error(`Request failed: ${reason}`);
  });
#A Creates a controller that allows us to abort a fetch before it finishes
#B Sends a request to an HTTP test endpoint that will respond after a 2-second delay
#C Creates a promise that will be rejected after a 1-second delay
#D Creates a promise that races the two given promises

In addition to Promise.race, this example introduces AbortController, an API introduced in ES2018 for canceling async operations. We wire up the controller to the fetch request by passing its signal property as an option, then call the controller’s abort() method to cancel the request. AbortController is an underused feature: without it, the fetch would continue in the background long after the timeout, consuming precious resources that we might need for other network requests.

Limiting concurrency with promise utilities

You may have noticed a significant limitation in all of the Promise methods for handling multiple promises: since they only return a single promise, they’re only suitable for dealing with a final (or, in the case of Promise.race, a first) concurrency event. They won’t help with scenarios that involve managing concurrency with constrained resources. For example, you might want to spawn Web Workers to perform a large number of tasks, but trying to spawn a Worker for every task at once would be impractical — you might run out of memory!

Happily, the prolific Sindre Sorhus has created a popular library for limiting concurrency called p-limit. You can use it with any task function that returns a promise. p-limit is part of an entire family of lightweight promise utility libraries that also includes p-throttle and p-debounce.

Let’s wrap up our discussion of promises by getting a precise answer to the question of when the promise handler fires.

8.1.4 Promise timing: of microtasks and macrotasks

We mentioned the event loop back in chapter 4. To recap: JavaScript is a single-threaded language, which means that events never interrupt code execution. Instead, they’re queued. When the JavaScript engine reaches the end of the code it’s running, it handles the next queued event (if there is one). This repeated process of running code and checking for queued events is known as the event loop.

That’s fine as a high-level description, but it’s short on specifics. Exactly what order do queued events fire in? Before we answer that question, let’s look at a concrete example:

Listing 8.6 — Queueing callbacks with setTimeout and thenJavaScript
setTimeout(() => {
  console.log("setTimeout callback");
}, 0);

Promise.resolve(true).then(() => {
  console.log("then callback");
});

console.log("end of script");

(This example was inspired by Jake Archibald’s classic 2015 blog post, “Tasks, microtasks, queues and schedules”. While some of the material in that post has fallen out of date, it’s highly recommended if you’re interested in seeing more interactive examples of the concepts in this section.)

If you run this script in any JavaScript environment, you’ll reliably get this output:

end of script
then callback
setTimeout callback

You might be surprised that the then callback ran after the end of the script, since the promise was already settled when its then method was called. However, promises never call the then callback synchronously. This is a blessing, since it makes the flow of code execution easier to predict: the code after the then call will always run before the callback.

That explains why end of script is first, but why is setTimeout callback last? Well, for one, setTimeout(callback, 0) is a bit of a misnomer: according to the HTML Living Standard, setTimeout has a minimum delay of 4 milliseconds. But even if the delay truly were 0 milliseconds, the then callback would fire first, because there are actually two event queues!

Promise callbacks live in what the ECMAScript spec calls the job queue, though it’s more popularly known as the microtask queue. By contrast, setTimeout callbacks live in what’s commonly referred to as either the task queue or, for contrast with the microtask queue, the macrotask queue. Events in the microtask queue are strictly prioritized over events in the macrotask queue. With that knowledge, we can describe the event loop more precisely:

  1. The JavaScript engine runs code until it reaches the end.
  2. If there’s anything in the microtask queue, it runs the next microtask.
  3. If there’s anything in the macrotask queue, it runs the next macrotask.

When then is called on a settled promise, it adds the callback to the microtask queue, which means that it’ll run before any pending timeouts, DOM events, and I/O events — all of which are macrotasks.

For many years, savvy JavaScript developers would take advantage of this feature of promises to trigger code that needed to run asynchronously but sooner than the likes of setTimeout would allow. For example, frameworks like React use microtasks to batch updates to the DOM before it’s rendered. (Although rendering isn’t performed by JavaScript, browsers time it as a macrotask.) Fortunately, there’s now a well-supported API that provides a more direct solution: queueMicrotask.

Timing according to the specs

ECMAScript 2015 introduced both promises and the notion of the job queue (aka microtasks), laying down strict rules for JavaScript engines to follow when timing promise callbacks. However, ECMAScript doesn’t define the rules for timing functions like setTimeout or queueMicrotask. Instead, those are defined in the HTML Living Standard. In principle, a JavaScript runtime could give those functions different behaviors or omit them entirely. But in practice, Node.js set a precedent of following the HTML spec for those timing functions, and other non-browser runtimes have followed suit.

That concludes our tour of promises. As you’ve seen, promises are a powerful API for interacting with asynchronous operations. But it gets better! You’re about to meet await, a keyword that works as a much sleeker alternative to then callbacks.

8.2 Flattening promise callbacks with await

When promises were first introduced, they were an immediate hit with developers. Even before they were added to the ES2015 specification, the then-ubiquitous jQuery library offered its own version of promises. JavaScript codebases were filled to the brim with chains of .then().

Today, promises are more popular than ever, yet you hardly see then used at all. Instead, you see await. The await keyword combines the power of promises with a simple syntax that resembles synchronous code. That combination of power and simplicity has made it a staple of modern JavaScript code.

In this section, we’ll describe the problem that await solves. Then we’ll take a peek under the hood and see exactly how it works as a replacement for the promise callback methods we learned about in the previous section. Lastly, we’ll introduce the await keyword’s close cousin, async.

8.2.1 The problem with nested callbacks

In chapter 3, we highlighted the ability to pass a function to another function as a callback as one of JavaScript’s greatest features. The simplicity and versatility of callbacks as an event-handling mechanism was a key reason that Ryan Dahl chose the language for the server runtime that would become Node.js.

But callbacks have a drawback: code that uses nested callbacks tends to become unreadable. Early Node.js developers would complain of “callback hell” when dealing with a series of async operations. For example, a web server’s HTTP endpoint might send an authentication request, query a database, then render the data into a template from disk, resulting in a series of callbacks like this:

Callback hellJavaScript
server.on("request", (request, response) => {
  authenticateUser(request, (authResult) => {
    if (!authResult.ok) {
      response.send(401, "Not authorized");
      return;
    }
    queryDatabase(request, (dbResult, dbError) => {
      if (dbError) {
        response.send(500, "Internal error");
        return;
      }
      renderTemplate("page.template", dbResult, (html) => {
        response.send(200, html);
      });
    });
  });
});

You could disentangle the callbacks by moving them to separate named functions rather than declaring them inline. But that introduces another form of complexity: in the nested structure, every previous callback’s arguments are available to every subsequent callback. In the de-nested structure, you’d need to find some other way to pass state around. Having to explicitly marshal state from one part of the application’s code to another is one of the problems that callbacks so elegantly solved!

Promises came along and offered more flexibility about where callbacks were defined, but the fundamental problem remained: if you wanted the state from previous callbacks to be available, you needed to either nest those callbacks or add boilerplate code to move state around.

Then ES2017 introduced the await keyword, and everything changed. With promise-based APIs and await, this series of asynchronous function calls can be expressed just as succinctly as if they were synchronous:

The same endpoint, with awaitJavaScript
server.on("request", async (request, response) => {
  const authResult = await authenticateUser(request);
  if (!authResult.ok) {
    response.send(401, "Not authorized");
    return;
  }
  try {
    const dbResult = await queryDatabase(request);
    const html = await renderTemplate("page.template");
    response.send(200, html);
  } catch {
    response.send(500, "Internal error");
  }
});

The result is much more readable, without losing any of the benefits of JavaScript’s event-driven single-threaded model.

But how does it work? Let’s take a look at the hidden secrets of await.

8.2.2 How await works

The expression await value implicitly converts the value to a promise according to the same promise resolution algorithm we discussed in section 8.1.1. The promise is equivalent to Promise.resolve(value). Then it halts code execution until that promise is settled. That means that the JavaScript engine will go to the next step of the event loop, checking for queued events as described in section 8.1.4. This is an important point: await is non-blocking, because other events are free to fire while its promise is pending.

When the promise is settled, it’ll queue a microtask (just like calling then) that does one of two things:

  1. If the promise was fulfilled, code execution will resume, with the await expression taking on the fulfilled value.
  2. If the promise was rejected, the rejection reason will be thrown from the await line.

Here are a few examples of await in action:

await in actionJavaScript
console.assert((await "Phantom Blade") === "Phantom Blade");
console.assert(
  (await Promise.resolve("Falling Devil")) ===
    "Falling Devil",
);
await Promise.reject(new Error("Deadly Mirage")); // throws

The rejection behavior is especially noteworthy here. Not only does await provide a succinct syntactic alternative to then, it also gives us more robust error handling, since the thrown error includes a complete stack trace — just like we’d get with synchronous code. This ability to throw errors addresses one of the biggest gripes that JavaScript developers had when promises were first introduced.

By the way, you may have noticed that we used await in the middle of an expression, pausing code execution at exactly that point. But that’s not all: we can use await in loops and conditions, too. Try doing that with then!

Of course, if await could be used anywhere in JavaScript code, it would break the long-held assumption of JavaScript developers that their code can’t be interrupted by events. Fortunately, the ECMAScript spec has a clever solution to this problem. The await keyword is only allowed to be used in either:

  • The top level of an ECMAScript module (ESM), or
  • A function declared with the async keyword

Thanks to these two rules, you can rest easy knowing that when you call a function, that function can’t use await to interrupt your code’s flow of execution. That’s true even if that function is an async function, for reasons that will become apparent in the next section.

ECMAScript modules will be a major topic in chapter 13. Long story short, you can declare a module as ESM by either specifying "type": "module" in the closest package.json or using the .mjs or .mts extension (for JavaScript or TypeScript, respectively) in the module’s filename. All of the example code for this chapter uses .mts, which means that you can play around with await freely — as long as you’re not inside of a function.

Note There’s no ESLint rule for identifying the use of await where it isn’t allowed. There doesn’t need to be, because it triggers a parser error. Running ESLint, TypeScript, or any other tool that parses your code will catch illegal awaits.

Next we’ll discuss the async keyword and find out what makes async functions special.

8.2.3 Automating promise creation with async

The magic of the await keyword is its ability to make consuming promises as easy as consuming synchronous values. The async keyword, conversely, makes it easy to produce promises. No need to call new Promise or any of the helper functions we’ve seen; instead, you can just return a value from a function. Let’s look at a simple example:

Listing 8.7 — Returning a simple value from an async functionJavaScript
const makeNinjaName = async () => "Ghost of Tsushima";  // #A
const ninjaNamePromise = makeNinjaName();
console.assert(
  (await ninjaNamePromise) === "Ghost of Tsushima",            // #B
);
#A Defines a function that wraps its return value in a promise
#B Unwraps the promise to get its fulfilled value

The async keyword is only used when defining a function. It works with both the function keyword and, as in the example above, with arrow functions. Functions defined in this way are simply called async functions. Here’s how they work:

  • Returned values are converted to promises using the same promise resolution algorithm described in section 8.1.1. That means that return value is equivalent to return Promise.resolve(value), except that value is returned as-is if it’s already a promise.
  • Thrown values are converted to rejected promises. In other words, throw error is effectively equivalent to return Promise.reject(error).

These behaviors guarantee that a call to an async function will always return a promise. In TypeScript, you can see this clearly by examining the return type of a function. The return type for makeNinjaName in the example above is Promise<string>, a promise whose fulfilled value is a string. (Note that a promise’s rejection reason always has the type unknown, just as the type of a caught error is always unknown. In both cases it’s considered a best practice to use Error objects, but this isn’t enforced by the type checker.)

We mentioned in the previous section that await can’t be used inside of a function unless that function is declared with async, since doing so would interrupt the flow of execution. The reason that it’s safe to use await inside an async function is the guaranteed return type. From the async function caller’s perspective, an await doesn’t interrupt their flow of execution; it only affects when and how the promise returned by the async function resolves.

Note There’s a helpful rule in typescript-eslint called promise-function-async that enforces that all functions that return a promise be declared with async. The main motivation for the rule is error handling: if the function returns a promise, the caller is likely to expect it to return a rejected promise rather than synchronously throwing an error.

Let’s tie our async and await discussion together with an illustrative example, this time rewriting listing 8.3 with more succinct, reusable code:

Listing 8.8 — Using an async function to fetch and parse JSONTypeScript
const fetchJson = async (url: string) => {        // #A
  const response = await fetch(url);                     // #A
  if (!response.ok) {                                     // #A
    throw new Error(`Status code ${response.status}`);      // #A
  }                                                       // #A
  return response.json();                                  // #A
};                                                        // #A

try {
  console.log(
    await fetchJson(                                       // #B
      "https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts/1",         // #B
    ),                                                      // #B
  );
} catch (error) {                                           // #C
  console.error(`Request failed: ${error}`);                  // #C
} finally {
  console.log("Request finished");
}
#A Defines an async function to fetch and parse JSON from the given URL
#B Calls the async function and logs the fulfilled value
#C Catches any errors thrown from the async function

Now you can see why developers have embraced async and await. Thanks to this convenient syntax, JavaScript APIs have gradually shifted away from callbacks and toward returning promises. Node.js, for example, offers both its classic fs module for file I/O and a newer fs/promises variant. It also provides a convenient promisify utility that can convert any function that uses a traditional Node.js-style callback into one that returns a promise — see util.promisify.

But a promise can only represent a one-time event. What if we want to interact with a multi-step process without using a callback? For that, let’s enter the world of generators.

8.3 Making interruptible loops with generators

Generators were introduced with much fanfare in ES2015, the same ECMAScript version that made promises an official part of the language. Generators and promises were expected to form a dynamic duo that developers would use to make nested callbacks a thing of the past. In a world of generators, async JavaScript code might look like this:

The generator future that never quite arrivedTypeScript
function* multiFetch(urls: string[]) {
  for (const url of urls) {
    yield fetch(url);
  }
}

It didn’t work out that way. Few developers took to the strange-looking syntax of generators. And when ES2017 introduced async and await, it took away what had been one of their major use cases. Today, generators are widely regarded as a bit of an oddity, useful for only a few niche scenarios. Still, it’s worth familiarizing yourself with them. Under the right conditions, generators can be a valuable tool to have in your JavaScript Ninja belt!

Before we get into generators themselves, we need to lay down some groundwork. Just as async is a convenient syntax for defining a function that returns a promise, generators are a convenient syntax for defining a function that returns an iterable. So let’s talk about iterables.

8.3.1 Iterables and iterators

We’ve mentioned ES2015 quite a few times in this chapter. Quite simply, ES2015 was a huge leap forward for JavaScript, introducing tons of new features. One of those new features was the for…of loop syntax:

A simple for…of loopJavaScript
for (const number of [1, 2, 3]) {
  console.log(number);
}

The for…of syntax is convenient for working with arrays, but it’s even more helpful for iterating over other collection types like maps and sets (which were also introduced by ES2015), where a traditional for loop isn’t an option. In fact, you can use for…of with any object that satisfies these conditions:

  1. The object must have the key Symbol.iterator. We haven’t talked about symbols (yet another ES2015 feature!), so here’s what you need to know: symbols are the only non-string type that can be used as object keys. They’re useful for differentiating special object properties. Symbol.iterator is one of a handful of symbols that are made available as static properties of the Symbol class. If you’re curious to learn more about symbols, see MDN.
  2. The value of object[Symbol.iterator] must be a function that returns an object with a next() method. Each time that method is called, it’s expected to return an object called an iterator result with properties named value and done.

When those conditions are met, the object is called an iterable, and the object returned by object[Symbol.iterator]() is an iterator.

Let’s make these concepts more concrete by drilling down on the previous example. Instead of using for…of, we’ll use the array’s iterator directly:

Listing 8.9 — Looping through an array using its iteratorJavaScript
const numbers = [1, 2, 3];
const iterator = numbers[Symbol.iterator]();   // #A
let iteratorResult = iterator.next();            // #B
while (!iteratorResult.done) {                     // #C
  console.log(iteratorResult.value);                  // #D
  iteratorResult = iterator.next();                // #E
}
#A Uses the Symbol.iterator key to access the array’s iterator object
#B Gets the first iterator result
#C Loops until the iterator result is in the done state
#D Logs the iterator result’s value
#E Gets the next iterator result

This is a very convoluted way to iterate through an array, but it demonstrates what’s going on under the hood in a for…of loop. It shows that there’s nothing magical about arrays: you can easily write your own iterable.

Before we do that, let’s talk about one other way that JavaScript uses iterables: destructuring. (Another ES2015 feature, by the way.) Consider this code, which assigns three values to three variables:

Iterable destructuringJavaScript
const [a, b, c] = ["a", "b", "c"];

This is commonly referred to as the array destructuring syntax. But it’s actually an iterable destructuring syntax! Under the hood, JavaScript is using the iterator to get each sequential value, allowing this syntax to be used for all kinds of collections. You can even use the spread or rest syntax to collect all of the iterable’s values:

Spread and rest with iterablesJavaScript
// Call a function with the spread syntax
func(...iterable);

// Convert an iterable to an array with the spread syntax
const array = [...iterable];

// Convert part of the iterable to an array using the rest syntax
const [first, ...others] = iterable;

If you do try to spread all of the iterable’s values, though, just be careful that the iterable is finite! Here’s an example of an iterable that most certainly isn’t:

Listing 8.10 — Defining a custom iterableTypeScript
const randomNumbers: Iterable<number> = {              // #A
  [Symbol.iterator]: () => ({                             // #B
    next: () => ({ value: Math.random() }),             // #B
  }),                                                    // #B
};

const [num1, num2] = randomNumbers;                      // #C
console.log(num1, num2);
#A The type annotation lets TypeScript verify that the object is iterable
#B Returns an iterator that generates random numbers
#C Calls the iterator twice and assigns each result value to a variable

As you can see, iterables aren’t limited to finite, static collections. They can be used to lazily generate values as needed. For that matter, who says they need to return values at all? That next() function could do anything, after all.

Now you should have a solid footing to understand iterables and why they’re useful. But defining custom iterables the way we did in listing 8.9 is awfully verbose! With that problem in mind, let’s meet generators.

8.3.2 Iterating within a function with generators

A generator function is defined using the function keyword followed by *. (Arrow functions can’t be generator functions.) Just like async functions, generator functions guarantee a particular return type. Specifically, a generator function always returns a generator object, which is both an iterable and an iterator: calling generator[Symbol.iterator]() returns generator itself.

Generator terminology

According to the ECMAScript spec, a function declared with function* is a generator function and the object it returns is a generator. Colloquially, though, you’ll often hear the term “generator” used to refer to both. That’s understandable, as the two are inextricably intertwined: there’s no way to create a generator without a generator function, or vice versa. We use the terms generator function and generator object throughout this section to try to clearly differentiate the two entities.

Here’s where things get interesting: each time the generator’s next() method is called, it advances the generator function until it either returns or uses yield. The yield keyword is a unique feature that’s only valid inside a generator function (figure 8.2). yield pauses the function’s execution, but unlike await, it doesn’t pause the entire JavaScript thread. Instead, execution jumps to where the generator’s next() method was called, just as it would if you used return. Calling the generator’s next() method again resumes code execution at the yield. In other words, the generator function picks up where it left off.

The iterator result returned from next() looks like this:

  • If the function hits a yield expression, the iterator result has the form { value, done: false }, where value is the value that comes after the yield keyword (or undefined if yield is used by itself).
  • If the function returns, the iterator result has the form { value, done: true }, where value is the value that comes after the return keyword (or undefined if return is used by itself or the function simply reached its end).
  • If the function throws an error, it gets thrown from the next() call.

There’s a lot to unpack there, so let’s start with a simple example: an adaptation of the random number iterable in listing 8.10 as a generator function.

Listing 8.11 — Defining an infinitely iterable generatorJavaScript
function* randomNumbers() {                            // #A
  while (true) {                                      // #B
    yield Math.random();                               // #B
  }                                                    // #B
}

const randomNumberGenerator = randomNumbers();          // #C
const [num1, num2] = randomNumberGenerator;             // #D
console.log(num1, num2);
#A Defines a generator function
#B Yields a new random value for every iterator result
#C Gets a generator object from the generator function
#D Iterates through the generator twice and collects the two values it yields

Just like await, yield pauses the function’s code execution while preserving its state. You can have as many yields as you like in a generator function.

An interesting but lesser-used feature of generators is the ability to pass a value into the next() method. When you do that, the yield expression that the generator resumes from will have the value that you passed in:

Listing 8.12 — A generator with two-way yieldTypeScript
function* multiplier(): Generator<number, unknown, number> {  // #A
  let number = 1;
  while (true) {
    const multiplier = yield number;                    // #B
    number *= multiplier;                                 // #B
  }
}

const multiplierGenerator = multiplier();
console.assert(multiplierGenerator.next().value === 1);
console.assert(multiplierGenerator.next(5).value === 5);
console.assert(multiplierGenerator.next(4).value === 20);
#A The type annotation lets TypeScript verify that the generator both returns and accepts a number
#B Yields the number, then multiplies the number by the value passed to next()

One more interesting feature is the ability to delegate to another generator using yield*. This means that the original generator will yield values from the delegated generator until those values are exhausted (that is, until done is true):

Listing 8.13 — Using yield* to delegate to another generatorJavaScript
function* warriors() {
  yield "Sun Tzu";
  yield* ninjas();                            // #A
  yield "Genghis Khan";
}

function* ninjas() {
  yield "Hattori";
  yield "Yoshi";
}

for (let warrior of warriors()) {
  console.log(warrior);
}
#A Delegates to another generator
Sun Tzu
Hattori
Yoshi
Genghis Khan

The output of this code shows that yield* ninjas() goes through all of the yields in ninjas before returning the flow of code execution to warriors.

A great use case for yield* is recursion: a generator can yield to another generator returned from the same generator function with different arguments. Using a recursive generator, you could iterate through all of the elements in a DOM tree in a simple for…of loop, without the inefficiency of converting the tree to a flat array.

Next we’ll find out what happens when we combine generators with the power of async and await.

8.3.3 Async iterables and async generators

So far we’ve seen how generator functions can pause their own execution using the yield keyword. But yield only moves the flow of code execution to where the next iterator result is consumed; it doesn’t pause the thread the way await does, allowing events to fire. That behavior wouldn’t make sense for an iterator.

That’s why ES2018 introduced async generators, along with corresponding async iterable and async iterator protocols. As you might have guessed, all of these constructs are built on top of promises: whereas a synchronous iterator’s next() method returns an iterator result object, an async iterator’s next() method returns a promise that fulfills with an iterator result object.

Async iterables are a straightforward analogue of synchronous iterables: instead of the key Symbol.iterator, they use the key Symbol.asyncIterator. (There’s nothing stopping an object from having both keys, making it both an iterable and an async iterable.) Calling object[Symbol.asyncIterator]() is expected to return an async iterator, an object with a promise-returning next() function.

But all of that is, thankfully, abstracted by async generators. To define one, you just use the async keyword with the now-familiar function* syntax:

Listing 8.14 — Using an async generatorTypeScript
async function* fetchPosts() {                        // #A
  for (let i = 1; i <= 3; i++) {
    const response = await fetch(                       // #B
      `https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts/${i}`,   // #B
    );                                                    // #B
    if (!response.ok) {                                   // #C
      throw new Error(`Status code ${response.status}`);    // #C
    }                                                     // #C
    const json = await response.json();
    yield json;                                          // #D
  }
}

for await (const post of fetchPosts()) {              // #E
  console.log(post);                                       // #E
}                                                        // #E
#A Defines an async generator
#B Uses await to pause while waiting for the response
#C Throws if the response’s status code indicates an error
#D Resolves the next iterator result promise
#E Iterates through the async iterator

By combining yield with async and await, we finally have the ability to actually pause code execution inside of a generator function!

In terms of how they’re consumed, async iterators aren’t quite as versatile as the synchronous variety: you can’t use them in array destructuring or spread them as function arguments. The only syntax that uses async iterators (apart from calling next() directly) is the for await…of loop syntax, an asynchronous analogue of for…of that waits for each iterator result promise to resolve.

Shortly after ECMAScript introduced async iterators, browsers introduced the ReadableStream API, a convenient way to read data as it flows in. Whenever you interact with a web-based LLM, that smooth flow of text is likely coming from a for await…of loop:

Reading a stream chunk by chunkJavaScript
for await (const chunk of stream) {
  // render the new chunk of text...
}

We’ll learn more about streams in chapter 11.

Now that you know how generators work, we come to a question that JavaScript developers have been pondering for years: are generators useful? The ability to pause a function and resume its execution later is a neat trick, but in practice, the main use case for generators is when you want to make some functionality easier to consume by wrapping it in an iterable. Using generators, you can neatly express:

  • Assigning multiple generated values using array destructuring.
  • A for…of loop that iterates through elements in a tree using recursion.
  • A for await…of loop that iterates through a series of expensive tasks.

The next time you find yourself writing a complex loop, ask yourself whether it might be more elegant to write it as a generator.

8.4 Summary

Nine things to remember

  1. A promise is a placeholder for the result of a task, typically an asynchronous one. A promise can either be fulfilled or rejected. Once that’s happened, we say that it’s settled: it will permanently remain in the same state.
  2. Asynchronous JavaScript APIs like fetch return a promise instead of taking a callback. We can attach as many callbacks as we want using the then method on the promise.
  3. We can use utility functions like Promise.all and Promise.race to combine promises for tracking multiple tasks.
  4. The await keyword waits for a promise to resolve, returning its fulfilled value or throwing its rejection reason.
  5. The async keyword guarantees that a function will always return a promise. When the function returns a value or throws an error, it’ll be used to resolve the returned promise.
  6. A generator function is declared by putting an asterisk (*) after the function keyword. Within the body of the generator, we can use the new yield keyword that yields a value and suspends the execution of the generator. If we want to yield to another generator, we use the yield* operator.
  7. The object returned by a generator function is an iterable. Iterables have a next() method for advancing to the next result, but are more often used in for…of loops or destructured like an array.
  8. The yield keyword works as a two-way binding with the generator’s next() method, allowing values to be returned from and passed into the generator.
  9. We can combine generators with async and await to produce async iterators that can be used in for await…of loops.

Source

Chapter 8, “Functions for the future: promises and generators”, of Secrets of the JavaScript Ninja, Third Edition (MEAP V10) — Manning Publications. Printed pages 154–183 of the PDF edition in this repository.

Both figures (8.1, 8.2) and all fourteen listings (8.1–8.14) are included above, with the book’s #A–#H callouts kept as annotation keys beneath each snippet.

Chapter 9

Objects, prototypes, and classes

This chapter covers

  • Object properties, getters, and setters
  • Proxying objects
  • Extending objects with prototypes
  • Building classes with inheritance

When we think of JavaScript objects, we tend to think of a set of key-value pairs, like JSON objects. But objects in JavaScript can be much richer than that. Their members can have special properties, like being read-only or excluded from iteration. They can be proxied to intercept certain calls. And most curiously of all, they offer a built-in inheritance mechanism known as a prototype, which can be modified at runtime to dynamically update the behavior of countless objects at once.

In the early days of JavaScript, prototypes were an essential feature of the language. Today, though, they’ve largely been supplanted by classes, which were introduced by ES2015. Classes provide a relatively simple and intuitive way to create different types of object, complete with inheritance. They’re also a better fit with TypeScript than the old prototypal inheritance model.

As a JavaScript Ninja, you may find yourself faced with challenges that involve all of these language features — even prototypes, which remain important to the behavior of objects even as their direct usage has fallen out of favor. To truly understand classes, you need to understand prototypes. With that in mind, let’s begin our journey into the world of JavaScript objects!

9.1 Customizing objects with properties

The primary way that we interact with objects in JavaScript is by reading and writing their properties. Consider the following code:

A plain propertyJavaScript
const ninja = { skillLevel: 100 };
console.log("Skill level:", ninja.skillLevel);

Here we define a ninja object with a property skillLevel. Later, if we want to change the value of that property, we can use a simple assignment like ninja.skillLevel = 110.

That’s all nice and convenient, but what happens in the following cases?

  • We want to prevent skillLevel from being modified directly.
  • We want skillLevel to be computed based on other factors when read.
  • We want to trigger other actions when the value of the skillLevel property is updated, such as logging the new value.

We can handle those cases elegantly using getter and setter methods.

9.1.1 Defining getters and setters

The terms getter and setter are used a bit loosely in JavaScript. Often, those terms refer to ordinary methods with the get and set prefixes:

Getters and setters by convention onlyTypeScript
const ninjaCollection = {
  ninjas: ["Yoshi", "Kuma", "Hattori"],
  getFirstNinja() {
    console.log(`Getting firstNinja: ${this.ninjas[0]}`);
    return this.ninjas[0];
  },
  setFirstNinja(ninja: string) {
    console.log(`Setting firstNinja: ${newNinja}`);
    this.ninjas[0] = ninja;
  }
};

These methods are getters and setters by convention. The naming has no effect on their functionality; it just conveys what they do to developers.

Distinct from that convention, getters and setters are a language feature that allow methods to be disguised as values. Let’s reimplement the above with proper getters and setters:

Listing 9.1 — Defining getters and setters in an object literalTypeScript
const ninjaCollection = {
  ninjas: ["Yoshi", "Kuma", "Hattori"],
  get firstNinja() {                                 // #A
    console.log(`Getting firstNinja: ${this.ninjas[0]}`);  // #A
    return this.ninjas[0];                            // #A
  },                                                // #A
  set firstNinja(newNinja: string) {                   // #B
    console.log(`Setting firstNinja: ${newNinja}`);       // #B
    this.ninjas[0] = newNinja;                          // #B
  },                                                // #B
};

console.assert(                                       // #C
  ninjaCollection.firstNinja === "Yoshi",              // #C
  "Yoshi is the first ninja",                       // #C
);                                                  // #C
ninjaCollection.firstNinja = "Hachi";                 // #D
console.assert(                                       // #E
  ninjaCollection.firstNinja === "Hachi" &&             // #E
    ninjaCollection.ninjas[0] === "Hachi",             // #E
  "Now Hachi is the first ninja",                    // #E
);                                                  // #E
#A Defines a getter method for the firstNinja property that returns the first ninja in our collection and logs a message
#B Defines a setter method for the firstNinja property that modifies the first ninja in our collection and logs a message
#C Accesses the firstNinja property as if it were a standard object property
#D Modifies the firstNinja property as if it were a standard object property
#E Tests that the property modification is stored
Getting firstNinja: Yoshi
Setting firstNinja: Hachi
Getting firstNinja: Hachi

This code may look very strange to you! We’ve defined two methods named firstNinja, but firstNinja is never called as a function. In fact, trying to call firstNinja() would throw an error. Instead, the two methods are called when firstNinja is accessed as a data property: reading ninjaCollection.firstNinja calls the get method, and assigning ninjaCollection.firstNinja = <value> calls the set method. That’s the power of get and set!

Getters and setters are powerhouse features. They allow JavaScript APIs to use “plain” objects with direct property access rather than the getX/setX boilerplate functions that proliferate in languages like Java, while giving developers the freedom to add actions such as validation, logging, or transforming the property from a different internal representation when those properties are used in the future.

The get and set keywords can only be used when defining a new object literal or class. If you want to define a getter or setter on an object that already exists, you’ll have to reach for another feature: Object.defineProperty. Listing 9.2 shows an example of using Object.defineProperty to add the same getter and setter as listing 9.1:

Listing 9.2 — Defining getters and setters dynamicallyTypeScript
interface NinjaCollection {                          // #A
  ninjas: string[];                               // #A
  firstNinja: string;                            // #A
}                                                // #A

const ninjaCollection = {                          // #B
  ninjas: ["Yoshi", "Kuma", "Hattori"],                 // #B
} as NinjaCollection;                                // #B

Object.defineProperty(ninjaCollection, "firstNinja", {  // #C
  get() {                                          // #C
    console.log(`Getting firstNinja: ${this.ninjas[0]}`);  // #C
    return this.ninjas[0];                            // #C
  },                                                // #C
  set(newNinja: string) {                              // #C
    console.log(`Setting firstNinja: ${newNinja}`);       // #C
    this.ninjas[0] = newNinja;                          // #C
  },                                                // #C
});                                                 // #C
#A TypeScript doesn’t infer types from Object.defineProperty, so we manually define a TypeScript type that incorporates the firstNinja property
#B Creates an object and uses the as keyword to assert that TypeScript should treat it as a NinjaCollection
#C Defines a property named firstNinja with a getter and a setter

As you can see, the Object.defineProperty is quite a bit more verbose than using the get and set keywords. But the ability to dynamically create getters and setters is very powerful! A common use case is testing, where you may want to permanently override a value attached to an object that you don’t directly control, such as window.location in a simulated DOM environment.

Unfortunately, using Object.defineProperty (or any other mechanism for adding new properties to an object) with TypeScript requires some extra effort, as seen in this example. One of TypeScript’s fundamental limitations is that the type of any variable is static, not dynamic: the same variable can’t have different types in different parts of the program. That means we face an awkward choice: either we leave ninjaCollection’s type as the type of the object literal that we first assigned to it (with no firstNinja property), or we override the type with as to tell TypeScript that it has a firstNinja property (even though it won’t have that property until later). We opted for the latter approach so that the type will be correct after Object.defineProperty runs.

There’s more to Object.defineProperty than just defining getters and setters. Let’s take a closer look.

9.1.2 Defining and redefining object properties

In listings 9.1 and 9.2, we defined a ninjaCollection object with the same getter and setter implementation for a property called firstNinja. But the two objects aren’t quite the same. If you were to run Object.keys on both objects, you’d get two different results: 

// Object from Listing 9.1
Object.keys(ninjaCollection)
> [ 'ninjas', 'firstNinja' ]

// Object from Listing 9.2
Object.keys(ninjaCollection)
> [ 'ninjas' ]

Both objects have a property called firstNinja, yet Object.keys acts as if that property doesn’t exist on the second object! The reason is that by default, properties created with Object.defineProperty aren’t enumerable. What that means is that they’re ignored by common mechanisms for iterating over an object. More precisely, non-enumerable properties are excluded from:

  • Object.keys, Object.values, and Object.entries
  • for…of and for…in loops
  • JSON.stringify
  • Object.assign and the spread syntax for copying object properties

JavaScript has always had non-enumerable properties. Take toString, for example: every object created with the object literal syntax has a toString method (inherited from the Object prototype, which we’ll learn about in section 9.3). Yet when you pass that object to Object.keys, toString is nowhere to be seen.

Being able to define non-enumerable properties is one of Object.defineProperty’s superpowers. And if you want a property to be enumerable, you can do so by passing enumerable: true as part of Object.defineProperty’s options object, known as the descriptor. We can modify listing 9.2 like so to make firstNinja enumerable:

Making the property enumerableTypeScript
Object.defineProperty(ninjaCollection, "firstNinja", {
  enumerable: true,
  get() {
    console.log(`Getting firstNinja: ${this.ninjas[0]}`);
    return this.ninjas[0];
  },
  set(newNinja: string) {
    console.log(`Setting firstNinja: ${newNinja}`);
    this.ninjas[0] = newNinja;
  },
});

A common pattern is to make data properties enumerable while making methods non-enumerable. That way, an object’s consumers can easily extract all of the data from the object (perhaps to serialize it as JSON) using const {...data} = object.

Symbols and enumeration

In section 8.3, we introduced symbols, a special type of value that can be used as an object key. Just like properties with string keys, properties with symbol keys can be defined with Object.defineProperty and made either enumerable or non-enumerable. However, symbol properties are ignored by loops and methods like Object.keys and JSON.stringify, even when they’re enumerable. The one place where being enumerable matters for a property with a symbol key is when copying that property with Object.assign or the spread syntax.

Let’s look at the descriptor object in more detail.

Accessor descriptors

A descriptor with a get or set method (or both) is called an accessor descriptor. An “accessor” is the technical term for a property that, when accessed, invokes a getter or setter.

If you set get but not set, the property will be read-only, triggering an error if a user tries to write to it:

A getter with no setterJavaScript
const obj = {};
Object.defineProperty(obj, "randomNumber", {
  get() {
    return Math.random();
  },
});
console.assert(
  typeof obj.randomNumber === "number",
  "A random number is always a number",
);
obj.randomNumber = 3; // TypeError

(If strict mode isn’t enabled, trying to write to a read-only property will fail silently. Yet another good reason to always use strict mode! See chapter 2 for more information on strict mode.)

Conversely, if your descriptor has set but not get, trying to read the property will yield undefined:

A write-only password propertyTypeScript
import crypto from "node:crypto";

const obj = {
  passwordHash: "",
};
Object.defineProperty(obj, "password", {
  set(newPassword: string) {
    this.passwordHash = crypto.hash("sha1", newPassword);
  },
});

obj.password = "12345";
console.assert(
  obj.password === undefined,
  "The password is read-only",
);
console.assert(
  obj.passwordHash.length === 40,
  "sha1 should produce a 40-char hash",
);

There are two options you can provide in an accessor descriptor: enumerable and configurable. We’ve already discussed enumerable, which defaults to false and determines whether various iteration syntaxes include the property. The configurable option determines whether the property definition itself can be changed. By default, it’s false, which means that the property definition is permanent: trying to overwrite it by either calling Object.defineProperty again or by using the delete keyword will cause an error to be thrown. If configurable is set to true, anyone with the object can easily overwrite the property:

A configurable propertyJavaScript
const obj = {};
Object.defineProperty(obj, "claim", {
  configurable: true,
  get() {
    return "This object belongs to the Uchiha Clan!";
  },
});

delete obj.claim;
obj.claim = "This object belongs to the Hyuga Clan now!";

And that’s all you need to know about accessor descriptors. Next let’s look at the other kind: data descriptors.

Data descriptors

Getters and setters are wonderfully versatile, but sometimes all you need is a simple value. You could, of course, set an object property to a value with direct assignment: object[key] = value. But perhaps you want to make that object property non-enumerable. Or you want to make it read-only, without the performance overhead of a getter function. In those cases, you can attach that value using Object.defineProperty with a data descriptor. At a minimum, a data descriptor provides a value:

A minimal data descriptorJavaScript
const obj = {};
Object.defineProperty(obj, "surfNinjaCount", {
  value: 3,
});
console.assert(
  obj.surfNinjaCount === 3,
  "There are 3 surf ninjas.",
);

As with accessor descriptors, properties defined with a data descriptor are non-enumerable and non-configurable by default. The same enumerable and configurable options are available to override those defaults.

Data descriptors offer one more option: writable. As with enumerable and configurable, writable defaults to false, which has the effect of preventing assignment. Trying to assign a new value to a non-writable property has the same effect as trying to assign a value to a getter with no setter: assuming you’re using strict mode, it causes an error to be thrown.

A data property that’s non-configurable and non-writable is effectively permanent. If it’s writable but not configurable, you can change the value but not other aspects of the property (for instance, you can’t make it enumerable or make it a getter/setter).

That wraps up our coverage of Object.defineProperty. It’s a handy API when you want to add getters and setters or non-enumerable properties to an object! But what if you want to add behaviors to an object without actually modifying the original? That’s coming up next as we introduce proxies.

9.2 Intercepting object access with Proxy and Reflect

A proxy is a surrogate through which we control access to another object. It enables us to define custom actions that will be executed when an object is being interacted with — for example, when a property value is read or set, or when a method is called. You can think of proxies as almost a generalization of getters and setters; but with each getter and setter, you control access to only a single object property, whereas proxies enable you to generically handle all interactions with an object, including even method calls.

We can use proxies when we’d traditionally use getters and setters, such as for logging, data validation, and computed properties. But proxies are even more powerful. Let’s look at an example:

Listing 9.3 — A proxy with a getter and setterTypeScript
const emperor = { name: "Komei" };
const representative = new Proxy(emperor, {                    // #A
  get: (target, key, receiver) => {                        // #B
    return key in target                                // #B
      ? Reflect.get(target, key, receiver)                  // #B
      : "Don't bother the emperor!";                      // #B
  },                                                       // #B
  set: (target, key, value, receiver) => {                 // #C
    if (!(key in target)) {                               // #C
      console.warn("Setting this key is impermissible.");   // #C
      return false; // Reject the operation              // #C
    }                                                      // #C
    return Reflect.set(target, key, value, receiver);        // #C
  },                                                       // #C
});

console.assert(
  representative.name === "Komei",
  "We can get the name property through a proxy",
);
representative.name = "Tenno";
console.assert(
  emperor.name === "Tenno",
  "We can set the name property through a proxy",
);
console.assert(
  // @ts-expect-error -- The nickname property is not
  // part of the object's type
  representative.nickname === "Don't bother the emperor!",
  "The proxy guards against improper gets",
);
#A Creates a new proxy with the emperor as its target
#B A getter that will be invoked when reading any property of the proxy
#C A setter that will be invoked when assigning to any property of the proxy

The first argument passed to new Proxy is an object called the target. The second argument is an object called the handler, with properties called traps that intercept various operations. The get and set traps intercept all property reads and assignments, respectively.

Reflect is a sibling API to Proxy that’s useful for passing operations through to a target object: Reflect.get(target, key, receiver) is equivalent to accessing target[key] with receiver as the value of this, and Reflect.set(target, key, value, receiver) is equivalent to setting target[key] = value with receiver as the value of this.

When you perform any operation on the proxy, the JavaScript engine checks to see if the proxy handler defines a trap for that operation. If there is, the trap function is executed and determines how the operation is handled, as shown in figure 9.2. If not, the operation goes through to the original object.

Proxies offer quite a few traps beyond get and set, including:

  • deleteProperty, which intercepts delete operations
  • ownKeys, which intercepts the key list operation used by Object.keys and for…in (among others)
  • defineProperty, which intercepts the operation performed by Object.defineProperty as well as simple assignment to a not-yet-existing property

For a comprehensive list of proxy traps, see the MDN docs.

This assortment of traps offers an extraordinary amount of control that simply isn’t possible with ordinary JavaScript objects, even with Object.defineProperty. One fascinating example of the power of proxies is Sindre Sorhus’ negative-array package, which uses a proxy to create an array where negative index values loop around to the end of the array, like in Python. (ES2022 added the at array method, which provides a more limited version of this behavior.)

In practical applications, proxies can be terrific for debugging and performance tuning: you can use the get trap to wrap each of an object’s methods with logging that records which method was called and how long it took to run. To do that, though, you need to be able to swap out the original object for a proxy. A JavaScript Ninja should consider that when architecting an application: using a centralized factory function for key objects makes it straightforward to return a proxy instead.

Even if you don’t use Proxy directly, you likely benefit from it when you write unit tests. Vitest and other popular testing frameworks use Proxy under the hood for their seemingly magical “automocking” functionality, where you can replace all of a module’s exports with your own functions or spies:

Automocking with VitestTypeScript
import { vi, expect } from "vitest";
import { multiply } from "./math.js";

// Replace all exports from math.js with equivalent spies.
vi.mock("./math.js", {
  spy: true,
});

test("spies records calls", () => {
  multiply(23, 42);
  expect(multiply).toHaveBeenCalledWith(23, 42);
});

Note JavaScript engines have to do a significant amount of extra work when they encounter a proxy. You should avoid using them in performance-critical paths in production code.

Now you’ve seen how custom properties and proxies can be used to give JavaScript objects uncommon behaviors. But there’s one kind of JavaScript object behavior that’s both very common and, in its own way, very strange: prototypal inheritance.

9.3 Dynamic inheritance with prototypes

When developing software, we strive not to reinvent the wheel, so we want to reuse as much code as possible. One form of code reuse that also helps organize our programs is inheritance, extending the features of one object into another. In the early days of JavaScript, the only way for developers to implement inheritance was by attaching prototype objects to constructor functions. Later, when classes were introduced by ES2015, they were built on the foundation laid by prototypes. This section will explain that foundation. Once you understand prototypes, you’ll be ready to master classes in section 9.4.

9.3.1 Fallbacks as inheritance

The idea of prototyping is simple: if an object property is referenced and the object itself doesn’t have that property, the JavaScript engine will fall back on that object’s prototype (if it has one). The process can repeat with a fallback to the prototype’s prototype, a process known as prototype chaining.

Let’s look at an example of this fallback behavior.

Listing 9.4 — With prototypes, objects can fall back on other objectsJavaScript
const yoshi = { skulk: true };                       // #A
const hattori = { sneak: true };                     // #A
const kuma = { creep: true };                       // #A

console.assert("skulk" in yoshi, "Yoshi can skulk");
console.assert(!("sneak" in yoshi), "Yoshi cannot sneak");
console.assert(!("creep" in yoshi), "Yoshi cannot creep");

Object.setPrototypeOf(yoshi, hattori);                   // #B
console.assert("sneak" in yoshi, "Yoshi can now sneak");     // #C
console.assert(
  !("creep" in hattori),
  "Hattori cannot creep",
);
Object.setPrototypeOf(hattori, kuma);
console.assert("creep" in hattori, "Hattori can now creep");   // #D
console.assert("creep" in yoshi, "Yoshi can also creep");     // #D
#A Creates three objects, each with its own unique property
#B Uses Object.setPrototypeOf to set one object as the prototype of another object
#C hattori’s sneak is used as a fallback for yoshi.sneak
#D kuma’s creep is used as a fallback for both hattori.sneak and yoshi.sneak

In this example, we start by creating three objects: yoshi, hattori, and kuma. Each has one specific property accessible only to that object: only yoshi can skulk, only hattori can sneak, and only kuma can creep. See figure 9.3.

You might be surprised to see inheritance with data properties. Unlike other languages, inheritance in JavaScript doesn’t make any distinction between data properties and methods. All properties are equally heritable.

To test whether an object has access to a particular property, we use the in operator. For example, executing skulk in yoshi returns true, because yoshi has access to the skulk property; whereas executing sneak in yoshi returns false.

In JavaScript, the object’s prototype property is an internal property that’s not directly accessible. Instead, we set it using Object.setPrototypeOf, which takes two object arguments and sets the second object as the prototype of the first. For example, calling Object.setPrototypeOf(yoshi, hattori) sets hattori as the prototype of yoshi, replacing yoshi’s existing prototype.

When we ask yoshi for a property that it doesn’t have, yoshi delegates that search to its prototype, namely hattori. That means we can access hattori’s sneak property through yoshi. See figure 9.4.

We can do a similar thing with hattori and kuma. By using the Object.setPrototypeOf method, we can set kuma as the prototype of hattori. If we then ask hattori for a property that he doesn’t have, that search will be delegated to kuma. In this case, hattori now has access to kuma’s creep property. See figure 9.5.

It’s important to emphasize that every object can have a prototype, and an object’s prototype can also have a prototype, and so on, forming a prototype chain. The search delegation for a particular property occurs up the whole chain, and it stops only when there are no more prototypes to explore. For example, as shown in figure 9.5, asking yoshi for the value of the creep property triggers the search for the property first in yoshi. Because the property isn’t found, yoshi’s prototype, hattori, is searched. Again, hattori doesn’t have a property named creep, so hattori’s prototype, kuma, is searched, and the property is finally found.

Note We’ve used Object.setPrototypeOf here to provide a clear demonstration of how prototypes are used. However, in production code, Object.setPrototypeOf should be avoided, as JavaScript engines optimize for objects whose prototype chains are set at creation time using constructors or the class keyword.

Is it the object’s own property?

Since prototypes are used as fallbacks, accessing object[key] doesn’t tell you whether that property is a property of object itself or of its prototype (or its prototype’s prototype, etc.). There are situations where we might care about that distinction. For example, we might use prototype inheritance to provide a configuration object with preset defaults, then take action if we see that one of those defaults was overridden directly on the object.

The Object prototype provides a method called hasOwnProperty that does exactly what it sounds like, taking a property key and returning true or false. But what if that property is, itself, overridden? To be on the safe side, the traditional solution in JavaScript is to call Object.hasOwnProperty.call(object, key), which is verbose but reliable. Happily, ES2022 introduced a more concise solution in the form of the static method Object.hasOwn(object, key).

Now that we have a basic idea of how the search for a particular property occurs through the prototype chain, let’s see how prototypes are used when constructing new objects with constructor functions.

9.3.2 Building prototyped objects with constructors

The simplest way to create a new object is with the object literal syntax:

An object literalJavaScript
const warrior = {};

The other, more versatile way is with the new operator and either a class or a constructor function. We’ll discuss classes in section 9.4. For now, let’s talk about constructors.

A constructor is any function that’s been written to be invoked with the new keyword. In chapter 6, we learned how new affects the meaning of the this keyword within the constructor function. Now that you know about prototypes, you’re ready for one more very important fact about the new keyword: the object returned from the constructor inherits the constructor function’s prototype. Let’s look at an example:

Listing 9.5 — Creating a new instance with a prototyped methodTypeScript
function Ninja() {}                                  // #A
Ninja.prototype.swingSword = () => true;                // #B

// @ts-expect-error -- Ninja has no construct signature  // #C
const ninja = new Ninja();                             // #D
console.assert(                                        // #D
  ninja.swingSword() === true,                        // #D
  "swingSword is inherited from the prototype.",       // #D
);                                                   // #D
console.assert(                                        // #E
  ninja instanceof Ninja,                             // #E
  "instanceof confirms that ninja is a Ninja",          // #E
);                                                   // #E
#A Defines a function that does nothing and returns nothing
#B Modifies the function’s built-in prototype object
#C Ignores a TypeScript error
#D Calls the function as a constructor, creating an object that inherits from the function’s prototype
#E The instanceof keyword tells us that Ninja’s prototype is in ninja’s prototype chain

Every time you create a function with the function keyword, that function receives an empty object as its prototype value, which is automatically inherited by any object created when that function is used as a constructor. (As you may recall, arrow functions can’t be used as constructors. For that reason, they don’t get a prototype value.) In short, for any function X, the expression new X creates an object whose prototype is X.prototype. See figure 9.6.

All of this may seem unnecessarily convoluted in a post-ES2015 world where the class keyword exists. And indeed, listing 9.5 could be written much more succinctly with class. But under the hood, class is doing the same thing: the class it creates is just a function with a prototype object.

Note that TypeScript doesn’t make it easy to do old-school prototypal inheritance like this: in order for the new Ninja() expression to run without an error, we’d have to define a separate type for objects returned from that constructor and then associate it with the Ninja function as a construct type. That’s because the prototype object could be modified at any time, so TypeScript needs us to tell it what the prototype’s final shape will be. By contrast, class types are inferred automatically.

An object with no prototype

When you create an object with the object literal syntax {}, the resulting object actually does have a prototype: Object.prototype. If you’ve ever wondered how ({}).toString() emits the string [object Object], it’s because of prototype inheritance!

ES5 introduced the Object.create(prototype) function for creating an object with the given prototype. The main use case for this method is Object.create(null), which creates an object with no prototype at all. Trying to access (Object.create(null)).toString() will throw an error. Prototype-free objects are recommended over {} in cases where an object is intended as a pure key-value store. However, the Map type (which we’ll discuss in chapter 10) is usually even better!

It’s worth taking a moment to reflect on how dynamic this form of inheritance is:

  • As we saw earlier, prototype properties are only used as fallbacks for properties that don’t exist directly on the object. That means that any method or value from the prototype can be overridden by setting a property with the same key on the object.
  • The prototype object can be modified to dynamically modify or add new methods or values, which will then be used as fallbacks for all objects with that prototype that don’t have those properties assigned directly.
  • The prototype of an object can be swapped out using Object.setPrototypeOf, as we saw earlier (though this is rarely used in practice).

In the early days of JavaScript, developers made vigorous use of this dynamism. For instance, a popular web library named MooTools added new features to the browser’s DOM APIs by modifying (among others) Element.prototype. These days, though, that kind of “monkey patching” is generally frowned upon. The more rigid approach to inheritance embodied by the class keyword and TypeScript has made code a lot more predictable. Still, there are cases where prototype modification can be a valuable tool, such as unit tests. For example, let’s say that you want to simulate a particular time zone:

Monkey-patching a built-in for testsJavaScript
// Normalize time zone in tests
Date.prototype.getTimezoneOffset = () => 120

// Later:
const date = new Date();
date.getTimezoneOffset(); // 120

Such overrides often create behavioral inconsistencies (changing getTimezoneOffset won’t affect the time zone shown when a date is formatted as a string, for example), but sometimes that’s the best you can do when it comes to testing!

Now that we have a grounded understanding of how prototypes work, let’s move on to classes.

9.4 Classic OOP with class and extends

JavaScript has always been a pastiche of a language. In computer science lingo, it’s multi-paradigmatic. If you want to use it as a straightforward procedural language like C, it can do that. If you want to use it as a functional language like Lisp, it can do that too. If you want to use it as an object-oriented language like Java… well, it’s right there in the name! With the introduction of classes in ES2015, classic object-oriented programming (OOP) became possible in JavaScript.

What makes JavaScript’s approach to OOP unique is the way its classes operate according to the same rules we’ve already seen for functions and prototypes. Let’s take a closer look.

9.4.1 Classes as shorthand for prototypes

Using the class keyword, we can succinctly define a constructor function along with a prototype. By convention, the names of classes (and constructor functions in general) are capitalized to differentiate them from other variables. Here’s a simple example:

Listing 9.6 — A simple classTypeScript
class Ninja {
  name: string;                                       // #A
  level: number;                                      // #A
  constructor(name: string, level: number) {           // #B
    this.name = name;                                 // #B
    this.level = level;                               // #B
  }                                                  // #B
  swingSword() {                                     // #C
    return true;                                      // #C
  }                                                  // #C
}

const ninja = new Ninja("Yoshi", 4);
console.assert(
  ninja instanceof Ninja,
  "The Ninja class is a constructor",
);
console.assert(
  typeof Ninja.prototype.swingSword === "function",
  "Instance methods belong to a prototype object",
);
console.assert(
  ninja.swingSword() === true,
  "Each instance inherits prototype methods",
);
console.assert(
  Object.hasOwn(ninja, "name"),
  "Properties assigned in the constructor belong to the instance",
);
#A TypeScript declarations for properties that instances of this class will have
#B Defines the class’s constructor function
#C Defines a prototype method

One bit of syntax that’s worth highlighting: constructor is a keyword, not a function name. Any other identifier would be treated as an instance function name. The constructor keyword defines the function that’s run by the expression new Ninja — which means that Ninja is, itself, the constructor function.

It should be noted that a class doesn’t need to have an explicit constructor. Having an empty constructor function is fine, too; it’ll construct an empty object that inherits the class’s prototype properties. If the class has a parent class (as seen in the next section), the parent’s constructor is inherited by default.

The instanceof keyword works by checking if the given function’s prototype is in the given object’s prototype chain. Be careful not to confuse it with typeof, which only tells you which basic type a given variable is. typeof will return "object" for any instance of any class. There is, however, a way to get the name of the class (or constructor function more generally) that an object was created from:

Getting an object’s constructor nameJavaScript
ninja.constructor.name; // "Ninja"

This works because any object created from a constructor function in JavaScript gets the constructor function itself assigned as its constructor property, and functions and classes receive a name property with their original identifier. It’s a handy trick for debugging, but not recommended for production code: it’s too easy to break the logic by renaming the function, or by running the code through a minifier that condenses names.

When we declare properties of a class as if it were an object literal, those properties become properties of the class’s prototype, to be inherited by all instances of the class. But we can also attach properties to the class itself using the static keyword:

Listing 9.7 — A class with a static methodTypeScript
class Ninja {
  name: string;
  level: number;
  constructor(name: string, level: number) {
    this.name = name;
    this.level = level;
  }
  swingSword() {
    return true;
  }
  static compare(ninja1: Ninja, ninja2: Ninja) {            // #A
    return ninja1.level - ninja2.level;                 // #A
  }                                                  // #A
}                                                    // #A

const ninja1 = new Ninja("Yoshi", 4);
const ninja2 = new Ninja("Hattori", 3);
console.assert(
  Ninja.compare(ninja1, ninja2) > 0,
  "The Ninja class can compare two ninjas",
);
#A Defines a property on the Ninja class itself

Now you know the ABCs of JavaScript classes. In the next section, we’ll start to take full advantage of OOP with inheritance.

9.4.2 Inheriting across classes

Just as prototypes can be chained, so too can classes using the extends keyword, creating a parent-child relationship:

Listing 9.8 — A class that inherits from a parentTypeScript
class Person {
  name: string;
  constructor(name: string) {
    this.name = name;
  }
  dance() {
    return true;
  }
}

class Ninja extends Person {                            // #A
  sneakiness: number;
  constructor(name: string, sneakiness = 3) {          // #B
    super(name);                                       // #B
    this.sneakiness = sneakiness;                      // #B
  }                                                  // #B
  sneak() {
    return `Sneak level ${this.sneakiness}`;
  }
}

const ninja = new Ninja("Chizu", 5);
console.assert(
  ninja instanceof Ninja,
  "A ninja is a ninja",
);
console.assert(
  ninja instanceof Person,
  "A ninja is also a person",
);
#A Declares a class that inherits from Person
#B Invokes the parent class’s constructor

When we create an instance of Ninja, it now inherits both the sneak method from Ninja and the dance method from Person via prototype chaining, as shown in figure 9.7.

The super keyword lets a class reference its parent class from anywhere in the class body. When used in the constructor, it runs the parent class’s constructor function against the same this that the child class is constructing. The child class isn’t required to call super in its constructor, but if it does, it must call super before it uses this.

Static properties are not inherited. If we wanted Ninja to have all of the same static properties as Person, we’d have to define them ourselves.

It’s worth noting that inheritance is linear in JavaScript. A prototype can only inherit from a single prototype, and a class can only inherit from a single class. There’s no notion of multiple inheritance.

JavaScript classes have one more feature that OOP connoisseurs will appreciate: private elements.

9.4.3 Restricting access with private elements

ES2022 introduced a syntax for making properties only accessible from within a class, the private element syntax. This syntax is only available in classes, not in normal JavaScript objects.

Any field name prefixed with # is private. These identifiers have some unique qualities, which is why the term “field” is preferred over “properties”:

  • Private fields can only be accessed using the dot syntax. So ninja.#greet works, but ninja["#greet"] would be undefined.
  • Private fields can only be accessed from within the class definition. Outside of that pair of curly braces, any attempt to reference those private fields will cause a syntax error.
  • Private fields can’t be proxied, enumerated, or deleted.

With those caveats in mind, private fields can be quite useful. A common use case is storing an internal value for a getter/setter pair. Even if you don’t care about unauthorized access, using the # syntax is nice for developer ergonomics: it makes it clear to readers which properties are internal, and it prevents IDEs from suggesting them as autocompletions externally.

Listing 9.9 — A class with private fieldsTypeScript
class Ninja {
  name: string;
  static #ninjas: Ninja[] = [];                            // #A
  constructor(name: string) {
    this.name = name;
    Ninja.#ninjas.forEach((ninja) => ninja.#greet(name));
    Ninja.#ninjas.push(this);
  }
  #greet(newNinjaName: string) {                        // #B
    console.log(                                          // #B
      `Greetings, ${newNinjaName}! I'm ${this.name}.`,     // #B
    );                                                   // #B
  }                                                      // #B
}

new Ninja("Kasumi");
new Ninja("Ryu");
new Ninja("Ken");
#A A static private field
#B A prototype-level private field

By the way, our example shows private fields at the static level and the prototype level, but it’s also possible (less commonly) to assign private properties directly to individual instances of the class, subject to the same limitation that the private properties can only be accessed within the class definition.

That wraps up our tour of objects, prototypes, and classes. With the tools in this chapter, you should be ready to tackle object-oriented programming like a JavaScript Ninja!

9.5 Summary

Thirteen things to remember

  1. We can use accessor methods (getters and setters) to run functions when properties are accessed or assigned.
  2. Accessor properties can be defined by using the built-in Object.defineProperty method or with a special get and set syntax as parts of object literals or ES6 classes.
  3. We can also use Object.defineProperty to control whether properties are writable or enumerable.
  4. With proxies, we can define custom actions that will be executed when an object is interacted with in any way.
  5. Proxy handlers for specific actions are called “traps.”
  6. The Reflect.get and Reflect.set methods allow us to perform property access from within a proxy trap while preserving the this context.
  7. Every object can have a prototype, an object to which we delegate the search for a particular property, if the object itself doesn’t have the searched-for property. An object’s prototype can have its own prototype, and so on, forming a prototype chain.
  8. Prototypes are closely linked to constructor functions. Every function has a prototype property that’s set as the prototype of objects that it instantiates.
  9. A function’s prototype object has a constructor property pointing back to the function itself. This property is accessible to all objects instantiated with that function and, with certain limitations, can be used to find out whether an object was created by a particular function.
  10. With the class keyword, we can define a constructor function and a prototype at the same time.
  11. The extends keyword creates a prototype chain where the parent class’s prototype is the fallback from the child class’s.
  12. Within a child class, the parent can be referenced with super.
  13. Fields whose names start with # are called private elements. They can only be referenced by using the dot syntax from within the same class in which they’re defined.

Source

Chapter 9, “Objects, prototypes, and classes”, of Secrets of the JavaScript Ninja, Third Edition (MEAP V10) — Manning Publications. Printed pages 184–212 of the PDF edition in this repository.

All seven figures (9.1–9.7) and all nine listings (9.1–9.9) are included above, with the book’s #A–#E callouts kept as annotation keys beneath each snippet.

Chapter 10

Dealing with collections

This chapter covers

  • Using array functions
  • Creating dictionaries with maps
  • Managing unique values with sets
  • How to preserve immutable collections
