Now that we’ve spent some time wrangling the particularities of objects in JavaScript, we’ll move on to a closely related topic: collections. We’ll start with arrays, the most common type of collection in JavaScript. We’ll explore some of the built-in array methods that allow you to take advantage of functional programming paradigms.

Next we’ll meet two newer collection types: maps and sets. Maps are collections of key-value pairs with capabilities beyond those of ordinary objects. Sets are collections of items in which no item can appear more than once.

Lastly, we’ll discuss mutability and why it’s often desirable for objects and collections to be immutable. We’ll see how TypeScript can guard against mutations with read-only types. We’ll also meet a popular package, Immer, that provides a convenient way to work with immutable objects and collections.

Let’s begin our exploration with the simplest and most common of all collections: arrays.

10.1 Arrays

If your programming background is in a typed language such as C, you might think of arrays as sequential chunks of memory that house items of the same type, where each chunk of memory is of fixed size and has an associated index through which you can easily access it.

Arrays in JavaScript are much more dynamic. Each item in an array can be of a different type. The size of the array can change at any time. And, most curiously of all, each array is also an object.

The dynamic nature of JavaScript arrays has some unfortunate side effects, particularly in terms of performance. But it also gives us convenience. Arrays come with a variety of built-in methods that will make our lives a lot easier.

Getting low-level with typed arrays

ES2015 introduced a variety of new types like Uint8Array and Int32Array that can be used to store raw data efficiently. They’re invaluable for niche applications like rendering graphics in WebGL. These typed arrays are completely different from traditional JavaScript arrays, with their own separate interfaces. Typed arrays are beyond the scope of this chapter, but they’ll make an appearance when we cover Workers in chapter 14.

We’ll start our tour of arrays by showing some of the different ways you can create them. Then we’ll explore how to add items to and remove items from different positions in an array. Finally, we’ll review some of the many methods that arrays provide.

10.1.1 Creating arrays

There are two basic ways to create a new array from scratch:

  • Using array literals, like []
  • Using the built-in Array constructor

Let’s start with a simple example in which we create an array of ninjas and an array of samurai.

Listing 10.1 — Creating arrays and manipulating lengthJavaScript
const ninjas = ["Kuma", "Hattori", "Yagyu"];    // #A
const samurai = new Array("Oda", "Tomoe");        // #B

console.assert(                                     // #C
  ninjas.length === 3,                              // #C
  "There are three ninjas",                       // #C
);                                                // #C
console.assert(                                     // #C
  samurai.length === 2,                             // #C
  "And only two samurai",                         // #C
);                                                // #C
console.assert(                                     // #D
  ninjas[0] === "Kuma",                            // #D
  "Kuma is the first ninja",                      // #D
);                                                // #D
console.assert(                                     // #E
  samurai.at(-1) === "Tomoe",                     // #E
  "Tomoe is the last samurai",                    // #E
);                                                // #E
console.assert(                                     // #F
  ninjas[4] === undefined,                         // #F
  "We get undefined if we try to access an out of bounds index", // #F
);                                                // #F

ninjas[4] = "Ishi";                               // #G
console.assert(                                     // #G
  ninjas.length === 5,                              // #G
  "Arrays are automatically expanded",              // #G
);                                                // #G

ninjas.length = 2;                                 // #H
console.assert(                                     // #H
  ninjas.length === 2,                              // #H
  "There are only two ninjas now",                  // #H
);                                                // #H
console.assert(                                     // #H
  ninjas[0] === "Kuma" && ninjas[1] === "Hattori",   // #H
  "Kuma and Hattori",                             // #H
);                                                // #H
console.assert(                                     // #H
  ninjas[2] === undefined,                         // #H
  "But we've lost Yagyu",                         // #H
);                                                // #H
#A To create an array, we can use an array literal []…
#B …or the Array constructor
#C The length property tells us the size of the array
#D We access array items with index notation: the first item is indexed with 0
#E The at method (introduced in ES2022) lets us access array items using negative indices, where -1 is the last item
#F Reading items outside the array bounds results in undefined
#G Writing to indexes outside the array bounds extends the array
#H Manually overriding the length property with a lower value deletes the excess items

In listing 10.1, we start by creating two arrays. The ninjas array is created with a simple array literal, and it’s immediately prefilled with three ninjas: Kuma, Hattori, and Yagyu. The samurai array is created using the built-in Array constructor.

When to use the Array constructor

JavaScript developers nearly always prefer the array literal syntax when creating new arrays. The Array constructor does have one niche use: when given a single numeric argument, that argument is interpreted as the length of the new array. (And yes, this is strange: new Array(5) creates an empty array of length 5, while new Array(5, 6) is equivalent to [5, 6]!)

The Array constructor is often used in conjunction with the fill method to assign the same value to every item. For example, new Array(100).fill("z") gives you an array of 100 z characters. You could achieve the same thing by starting with an empty array and calling array.push("z") 100 times in a loop, but the Array constructor approach is more efficient because the JavaScript engine never has to resize the array.

As you probably know, you access array items by using index notation, where the first item is positioned at index 0 and the last item at index array.length – 1. But if we try to access an index outside those bounds — like with ninjas[4] in our example — we won’t get the scary “Array index out of bounds” exception that we receive in most other programming languages. Instead, undefined is returned, signaling that there’s nothing there.

This behavior is a consequence of the fact that JavaScript arrays are objects. Just as we’d get undefined if we tried to access a nonexistent object property, we get undefined when accessing a nonexistent array index. On the other hand, if we try to write to a position outside of array bounds, as in ninjas[4] = "Ishi", the array will expand to accommodate the new situation. As shown in figure 10.1, adding a new element at index 4 creates a hole in the array, since there’s no item at index 3. Despite the missing item, the length property now reports a value of 5. The length property always reflects the highest index in the array: since the highest index is 4, the length is 5.

What exactly does it mean for index 3 to have no item? If you access ninjas[3], you’ll get undefined. But technically speaking, there’s no value at all at that point in the array — not even undefined. Iterators like the forEach method will skip over that index until you assign a value to it.

The length property of an array can be modified to change the array’s length. Setting a value higher than the current length will expand the array with empty items, whereas setting a value lower than the current length will trim the array from the end, as we did with ninjas.length = 2 in our example.

Now that we’ve gone through the basics of array creation, let’s go through some of the most common array methods.

10.1.2 Adding and removing items at either end of an array

Let’s start with the following simple methods we can use to add items to and remove items from an array:

  • push adds an item to the end of the array.
  • pop removes an item from the end of the array.
  • shift removes an item from the beginning of the array.
  • unshift adds an item to the beginning of the array.

Notice once again how versatile JavaScript’s dynamic arrays are. Using push and pop, an array can function as a stack (last in, first out). Using push and shift, an array can function as a queue (first in, first out).

Listing 10.2 — Adding and removing array itemsJavaScript
const ninjas = [];
ninjas.push("Kuma");                               // #A
console.assert(
  ninjas[0] === "Kuma",
  "Kuma is the first item in the array",
);

ninjas.push("Hattori");                            // #B
console.assert(ninjas[0] === "Kuma", "Kuma is still first");
console.assert(
  ninjas[1] === "Hattori",
  "Hattori is added to the end of the array",
);

ninjas.unshift("Yagyu");                           // #C
console.assert(
  ninjas[0] === "Yagyu",
  "Now Yagyu is the first item",
);
console.assert(
  ninjas[1] === "Kuma",
  "Kuma moved to the second place",
);
console.assert(
  ninjas[2] === "Hattori",
  "And Hattori to the third place",
);

const poppedNinja = ninjas.pop();                    // #D
console.assert(
  poppedNinja === "Hattori",
  "We've removed Hattori from the end of the array",
);
console.assert(
  ninjas[0] === "Yagyu",
  "Now Yagyu is still the first item",
);
console.assert(
  ninjas[1] === "Kuma",
  "Kuma is still in second place",
);

const shiftedNinja = ninjas.shift();                  // #E
console.assert(
  shiftedNinja === "Yagyu",
  "We've removed Yagyu from the beginning of the array",
);
console.assert(
  ninjas[0] === "Kuma",
  "Kuma has shifted to the first place",
);
#A Pushes a new item to the end of the array
#B Pushes another item to the end of the array
#C Unshifts an item to the beginning of the array
#D Pops the last item from the array
#E Shifts the first item from the array. Other items are moved to the left accordingly.

Figure 10.2 shows how push, pop, shift, and unshift modify arrays.

Note Under the hood, adding or removing an item to an array typically requires subsequent items to be moved in memory. That means that unshift and shift can be very expensive operations for large arrays, whereas push and pop are fast regardless of array size.

10.1.3 Adding and removing items at any array location

We’ve seen how items can be removed from the start and end of an array using the shift and pop methods, respectively. But what if we remove them using the delete operator instead?

Unlike the unshift and shift methods, the delete operator doesn’t cause later items to move. It just leaves an empty slot in place of the deleted item, as shown in figure 10.3.

Listing 10.3 — Deleting an array itemJavaScript
const ninjas = ["Yagyu", "Kuma", "Hattori"];

delete ninjas[1];                                // #A
console.assert(                                     // #B
  ninjas.length === 3,                              // #B
  "Length still reports that there are 3 items",     // #B
);                                                // #B
console.assert(
  ninjas[0] === "Yagyu",
  "First item is Yagyu",
);
console.assert(
  ninjas[1] === undefined,
  "Second item is empty",
);
console.assert(
  ninjas[2] === "Hattori",
  "Third item is Hattori",
);
#A Deleting an item with the delete operator
#B The array’s length is unchanged

What if we want to remove an item from an array and shift other items to fill the gap? Or conversely, what if we want to insert an item between existing items in an array? JavaScript provides an array method that’s versatile enough to do both: splice.

Listing 10.4 — Removing and adding items at arbitrary positionsJavaScript
const ninjas = ["Yagyu", "Kuma", "Hattori", "Fuma"];

let removedItems = ninjas.splice(1, 1);           // #A
console.assert(                                     // #B
  removedItems.length === 1,                          // #B
  "One item was removed",                          // #B
);                                                // #B
console.assert(removedItems[0] === "Kuma");            // #B
console.assert(                                     // #C
  ninjas.length === 3,                              // #C
  "There are now three items in the array",         // #C
);                                                // #C
console.assert(                                     // #C
  ninjas[2] === "Fuma",                             // #C
  "And Fuma is now the third item",                 // #C
);                                                // #C

removedItems = ninjas.splice(                       // #D
  1,                                              // #D
  2,                                              // #D
  "Mochizuki",                                     // #D
  "Yoshi",                                         // #D
  "Momochi",                                       // #D
);                                                 // #D
console.assert(
  removedItems.length === 2,
  "We've just removed two items",
);
console.assert(
  ninjas.length === 4,
  "There are now four items in the array",
);
console.assert(
  ninjas[0] === "Yagyu",
  "Yagyu is still here",
);
console.assert(                                     // #E
  ninjas[1] === "Mochizuki" &&                     // #E
    ninjas[2] === "Yoshi" &&                       // #E
    ninjas[3] === "Momochi",                       // #E
  "The new ninjas were added after Yagyu",          // #E
);                                                // #E
#A Uses splice at index 1 to remove one item
#B splice returned an array containing the removed item
#C The items after the removed item have moved to fill the gap
#D Uses splice at index 1 to remove two items and add three new items
#E The new items were inserted starting at the splice index

As you can see, the splice method takes three arguments: the index from which the splicing starts, the number of elements to be removed, and an array of items to add. If only two arguments are specified, no items are added. If only one argument is specified, all items from that index to the end of the array are removed.

Be careful not to confuse splice with its cousin slice, which returns a partial copy of the array:

slice returns a copy, not a mutationJavaScript
const ninjas = ["Yagyu", "Kuma", "Hattori", "Fuma"];
const middleNinjas = ninjas.slice(1, 3);        // #A
console.assert(
  ninjas.length === 4,
  "The original array was not modified"
);
console.assert(
  middleNinjas[0] === "Kuma" &&
    middleNinjas[1] === "Hattori",
  "The first and last ninjas were not copied"
);
#A Copies ninjas from index 1 up to (but not including) index 3 into a new array

Traditionally, a common use for slice was copying an entire array: const arrayCopy = array.slice(0). These days, though, developers tend to use the spread syntax: const arrayCopy = [...array].

Now that we’ve given you a refresher on how arrays work, let’s continue by studying some common operations that are often performed on arrays. These will help you write more elegant array-handling code.

10.1.4 Common operations on arrays

In this section, we’ll explore some of the most common operations on arrays:

  • Iterating (or traversing) through arrays
  • Mapping existing array items to create a new array based on them
  • Testing array items to check whether they satisfy certain conditions
  • Finding specific array items
  • Aggregating arrays and computing a single value based on array items (for example, calculating the sum of an array)

We’ll start with the basics: array iterations.

Iterating over arrays

One of the most common operations is iterating over an array. For traditionalists, JavaScript offers the classic for loop, which should feel familiar if you’ve worked in a language with a C-like syntax before:

A classic for loopJavaScript
const ninjas = ["Yagyu", "Kuma", "Hattori"];
for (let i = 0; i < ninjas.length; i++) {
  console.assert(ninjas[i] !== null, "ninja is not null");
}

ES2015 introduced the for…of syntax, which we met when discussing iterables in chapter 8. It’s a convenient alternative to for when you want to iterate over an array’s values and don’t care about their keys:

for…ofJavaScript
const ninjas = ["Yagyu", "Kuma", "Hattori"];
for (const ninja of ninjas) {
  console.assert(ninja != "null", "ninja is not null");
}

If you want to iterate over an array’s items as key-value pairs, you can use the entries iterator:

Iterating with entries()JavaScript
for (const [index, ninja] of ninjas.entries()) {
  console.assert(ninja != "null", `ninja ${index} is not null`);
}

Note An easy mistake devs make is using for…in (iterating over keys) when they meant to use for…of (iterating over values). Using for…in with an array is particularly strange: it would iterate over all of the array’s indices and any object properties attached to the array. Thankfully, typescript-eslint offers a no-for-in-array rule to catch this mistake.

Arrays also offer an iteration method, forEach, a pattern borrowed from functional languages like Scheme:

forEachJavaScript
const ninjas = ["Yagyu", "Kuma", "Hattori"];
ninjas.forEach((ninja) => {
  console.assert(ninja !== null, "ninja is not null");
})

Compared to for and for…of, using forEach for iteration has some noteworthy limitations:

  • In a for or for…of loop, you can use break or return to exit the loop early. With forEach, you’re committed to iterating through the entire array. Returning a value from the callback would have no effect. The one trick you could use to bail out early would be to throw an error.
  • A for or for…of loop can be made asynchronous by using await inside, as seen in chapter 8. With forEach, every iteration runs synchronously. (You could pass an async function as a callback, but the next iteration would start immediately after it returns its promise, rather than waiting for that promise to be settled.)

Note Using an async callback in forEach is one of many mistakes that typescript-eslint’s invaluable no-misused-promises rule can catch.

Because of these limitations, forEach has been relegated to a niche: it’s handy if you have a callback that you want to reuse for multiple arrays, but otherwise, developers tend to prefer for…of. forEach does have several siblings, though, and they’re far more useful! Let’s take a look at those other array iteration methods.

Mapping arrays

Imagine that you have an array of ninja objects. Each ninja has a name and a favorite weapon, and you want to extract an array of weapons from the ninjas array. You could use a for…of loop to push each weapon to the new array, like this:

Extracting weapons with a loopJavaScript
const ninjas = [
  {name: "Yagyu", weapon: "shuriken"},
  {name: "Yoshi", weapon: "katana"},
  {name: "Kuma", weapon: "wakizashi"}
];
const weapons = [];
for (const ninja of ninjas) {
  weapons.push(ninja.weapon);
}

But there’s a better way! The map method is a convenient way to derive a new array from an existing array, where each element in the new array is based on the corresponding element in the existing array.

Like forEach, the map method passes each item in its array to the given callback. In our example, it passes a ninja object, which we extract the weapon from using destructuring. (If you need a refresher on destructuring syntax, see MDN.) Since the callback is an arrow function with no curly braces, we can omit the return keyword.

The big difference between forEach and map is the return value: after invoking the callback with every item in the array, it returns a new array made up of all of the values returned from the callback. By contrast, forEach doesn’t return anything. The inner workings of map are shown in figure 10.4.

Listing 10.5 — Deriving an array with mapJavaScript
const ninjas = [
  { name: "Yagyu", weapon: "shuriken" },
  { name: "Yoshi", weapon: "katana" },
  { name: "Kuma", weapon: "wakizashi" },
];

const weapons = ninjas.map(({ weapon }) => weapon);  // #A
console.assert(
  weapons[0] === "shuriken" &&
    weapons[1] === "katana" &&
    weapons[2] === "wakizashi",
  "Every ninja's weapon is included",
);
#A Using map with destructuring to extract the weapon property from each ninja

Next we’ll look at a more powerful variant on map: flatMap.

One-to-many array transformations with flatMap

The map method is convenient when we want to do a 1:1 conversion from one array to another. But what if we want to omit some items, or insert additional items? Traditionally, that required either a traditional loop, a reduce (and inevitable arguments about code readability), or a chain of multiple array methods. In particular, developers figured out pairing map with a method called flat made for a powerful combination.

The flat method flattens an array, meaning that it takes nested arrays and replaces them with their elements. By default, it does this by just one level, meaning that [[1], [2, [3]]].flat() becomes [1, 2, [3]]. You can, optionally, specify the number of levels as an argument, which is effectively equivalent to calling flat that number of times.

Here’s the trick: if we use map with a callback that returns an array for each item, then use flat, the combination allows each item in the original array to map to an arbitrary number of items in the new array. In response to this popular pairing, ES2019 introduced flatMap, allowing the two-step process to be performed in a single optimized operation. Here’s an example that generalizes listing 10.5 to allow ninjas to carry multiple weapons, or no weapons at all:

Listing 10.6 — Deriving an array with flatMapJavaScript
const ninjas = [
  { name: "Yagyu", weapons: ["shuriken", "kunai"] },
  { name: "Yoshi", weapons: [] },
  { name: "Kuma", weapons: ["katana", "tanto"] },
];

const weapons = ninjas.flatMap(({ weapons }) => weapons);  // #A
console.assert(
  weapons[0] === "shuriken" &&
    weapons[1] === "kunai" &&
    weapons[2] === "katana" &&
    weapons[3] === "tanto",
  "All ninja weapons are included",
);
#A Using flatMap with destructuring to extract the weapons property from each ninja

With flatMap, the callback returns an array of items to add to the result array. In listing 10.6, we’re simply appending each ninja’s weapons to the aggregate weapons array.

As a JavaScript developer, there will be many times when you’d like to use a map but it won’t quite work because you need to skip some items or insert some additions. Traditionally, that’s driven developers to use reduce, a versatile array method that we’ll encounter later in the chapter. But once you get in the habit of using flatMap, you’ll find it to be a more elegant (and potentially more performant) solution to those problems.

Next we’ll see how we can test arrays to see if they meet certain conditions.

Testing array item conditions

When working with collections of items, you’ll often run into situations where you need to know whether all or at least some of the array items satisfy certain conditions. You could, again, do that with a for…of loop:

Testing with a loopJavaScript
let allNinjasAreNamed = true;
for (const ninja of ninjas){
  if (!("name" in ninja)) {
    allNinjasAreNamed = false;
    break;
  };
}

But JavaScript offers a more convenient alternative in the form of the every method, shown in this example along with the closely related some:

Listing 10.7 — Testing array item conditions with the every and some methodsJavaScript
const ninjas = [
  { name: "Yagyu", weapon: "shuriken" },
  { name: "Yoshi" },
  { name: "Kuma", weapon: "wakizashi" },
];

const allNinjasAreNamed = ninjas.every(              // #A
  (ninja) => "name" in ninja,                       // #A
);                                                   // #A
const allNinjasAreArmed = ninjas.every(              // #A
  (ninja) => "weapon" in ninja,                     // #A
);                                                   // #A
console.assert(allNinjasAreNamed, "Every ninja has a name");
console.assert(
  !allNinjasAreArmed,
  "But not every ninja is armed",
);

const someNinjasAreArmed = ninjas.some(            // #B
  (ninja) => "weapon" in ninja,                     // #B
);                                                   // #B
console.assert(
  someNinjasAreArmed,
  "But some ninjas are armed",
);
#A The every method takes a callback that’s called for each array item. It returns true if the callback returns a true value for all array items, or false otherwise.
#B The some method also takes a callback. It returns true if the callback returns a true value for at least one array item, or false otherwise.

The every method takes a callback that, for each item in the array, returns a value that indicates whether that item satisfies the condition. every returns true only if the passed-in callback returns a truthy value for every item in the array, or if the array is empty. Unlike forEach and map, it doesn’t blindly iterate over every item: if the callback returns false for any item, it bails out early.

Truthy and falsy values

JavaScript’s predilection for implicit conversion extends to the condition callbacks used by every and some: anything you return is implicitly converted to a boolean. That’s why it’s important to be aware of which JavaScript values are “truthy” (convert to true) and which are “falsy” (convert to false). The most common falsy values are null, undefined, 0, and "". For a complete list, see MDN.

The some method works similarly, taking a callback and iterating over all items until that callback returns a truthy value. If the callback returns a truthy value for some item, some stops there and returns true. Otherwise, it returns false.

Note Iterating over large arrays can incur significant overhead as the system pages through memory. For that reason, it’s often more efficient to use a custom loop that iterates through an array once instead of using separate iterators for individual checks, like the multiple every calls in listing 10.7.

Next we’ll explore how to search an array to find a particular item.

Searching and filtering arrays

Another common array operation is searching for an item, or constructing a new array with a subset of an array’s items. We can do both with the find and filter methods.

Listing 10.8 — Finding and filtering array itemsJavaScript
const ninjas = [
  { name: "Yagyu", weapon: "shuriken" },
  { name: "Yoshi" },
  { name: "Kuma", weapon: "wakizashi" },
];

const ninjaWithWakizashi = ninjas.find((ninja) => {      // #A
  return ninja.weapon === "wakizashi";               // #A
});                                                  // #A
console.assert(
  ninjaWithWakizashi?.name === "Kuma" &&              // #B
    ninjaWithWakizashi.weapon === "wakizashi",
  "Kuma is wielding a wakizashi",
);

const ninjaWithKatana = ninjas.find((ninja) => {
  return ninja.weapon === "katana";
});
console.assert(
  ninjaWithKatana === undefined,
  "We couldn't find a ninja that wields a katana",
);

const armedNinjas = ninjas.filter(                   // #C
  (ninja) => "weapon" in ninja,                        // #C
);                                                   // #C
console.assert(
  armedNinjas[0].name === "Yagyu" &&
    armedNinjas[1].name === "Kuma",
  "Yagyu and Kuma are armed",
);
#A The find method returns the first array item that satisfies the callback condition
#B The value returned by find could be undefined, so we use the optional chaining operator (?.) to access name safely
#C The filter method returns an array of all items that satisfy the callback condition

As with the condition callbacks for every and some, any returned from the callbacks for find and filter is implicitly converted to a boolean. Figures 10.5 and 10.6 show the inner workings of the find and filter functions.

Next we’ll go beyond simple iteration methods and into the realm of sorting.

Sorting arrays

One of the most common array operations is sorting — arranging items systematically in some order. JavaScript arrays have a built-in sort method, whose usage looks something like this:

The shape of a sort callbackJavaScript
array.sort((a, b) => a – b);

That callback is known as the compare function. It takes two items from the array as its arguments and returns a number:

  • If a callback returns a value less than 0, then item a should come before item b.
  • If a callback returns a value greater than 0, then item a should come after item b.
  • If a callback returns a value equal to 0, then items a and b are considered equivalent for sorting purposes.

And that’s about all you need to know about sort! The specific sorting algorithm is left up to the underlying JavaScript engine. Let’s look at a simple example.

Listing 10.9 — Sorting an arrayJavaScript
const ninjas = [
  { name: "Yoshi" },
  { name: "Yagyu" },
  { name: "Kuma" },
];

const collator = new Intl.Collator();                  // #A
ninjas.sort((ninja1, ninja2) =>                        // #B
  collator.compare(ninja1.name, ninja2.name),          // #B
);                                                   // #B
console.assert(
  ninjas[0].name === "Kuma" &&
    ninjas[1].name === "Yagyu" &&
    ninjas[2].name === "Yoshi",
  "The ninjas are now in alphabetical order",
);
#A Creates a collator that’s configured for the user’s locale
#B Sorts the ninja array in-place using the collator’s compare function

In older JavaScript code, you might see string comparisons like string1 < string2, which works by comparing character codes. That works reasonably well for strings consisting only of English letters, but goes off the rails in the vast world of Unicode. For that reason, using Intl.Collator is strongly preferred: it generates a collator object that’s tailored to the user’s locale, with a compare method that’s conveniently designed to be used in a sort callback. It can also be configured with options that let you control how to handle casing, numbers, and punctuation. For details on customizing collators, see MDN.

Note Strings offer a built-in localeCompare method that offers the same functionality as Intl.Collator, but there’s a catch: internally, it goes through the same initialization process as Intl.Collator on every call. Creating a collator once and reusing it for every comparison is much more efficient.

Notice that, like splice, the sort method modifies the array that it’s called on. It also returns that same array, which has been a source of confusion to many developers: if you see code like const sortedArray = array.sort(…), sortedArray is just a reference to array! If you want to leave the original array alone, the traditional solution is to duplicate the array and then sort the duplicate. ES2023 introduced a more elegant solution in the form of the toSorted method, which works like sort without modifying the original array.

Accumulating a value with reduce

Let’s say that you want to take the sum of all numbers in an array. You could write a loop:

Summing with a loopJavaScript
const numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4];
let sum = 0;
for (const number of numbers) {
  sum += number;
}
console.assert(sum === 10, "The sum of all numbers is 10");

That code is perfectly clear, but if you feel like putting on your functional programming hat, you can use reduce instead:

Listing 10.10 — Aggregating items with reduceJavaScript
const numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4];
const sum = numbers.reduce(                        // #A
  (acc, number) => acc + number,                  // #A
  0,                                             // #A
);                                                // #A
console.assert(sum === 10, "The sum of all numbers is 10");
#A Uses reduce to accumulate a single value from an array

The reduce method takes a callback and a value (in this case, 0). The value is used as the initial value of the accumulator. Then it iterates through the array, calling the callback with the accumulator (commonly written as acc) and the current array item as arguments. The value returned by the callback becomes the accumulator value for the next iteration. After the last iteration, the final accumulator value is returned.

It can be difficult to wrap your head around reduce at first. Some developers consider it an overly “fancy” way to write a loop. But you will see it out in the wild quite a bit, so it’s worth taking the time to understand it. Figure 10.7 sheds more light on the process.

What makes the reduce method so flexible is that it lets you use any kind of value as the accumulator: it can be an object, a map, a buffer, or anything else that you might want to generate from an array. That ability to generate complex data types in a single expression is why some developers love reduce.

Note If you’re not a fan of reduce, Sindre Sorhus has you covered with eslint-plugin-unicorn’s no-array-reduce rule.

That wraps up our coverage of arrays. There are still other array methods to discover, and nearly every new ECMAScript spec adds more! You can find a comprehensive list at MDN. Let’s move on to two other powerful collection types: maps and sets.

10.2 Maps

In chapter 9, we discussed how objects are more than just key-value pairs. And yet that’s often how they’re used, and understandably so: JavaScript’s syntax makes it very convenient to assign values to keys on an object and then access those values later.

But there are pitfalls with using objects this way. For one, as we saw in chapter 9, objects inherit from prototypes in a way that can make it difficult to tell exactly what’s “in” the object. You can mitigate that problem by creating a prototype-free object with Object.create(null) instead of using the object literal syntax.

A bigger problem is the limited nature of object keys: any time you write object[key], that key is implicitly converted to a string. (This is true for arrays, too: array[1] and array["1"] are equivalent!) The one exception is symbols, which we touched on briefly in chapter 8: the power of symbols is that they work as object keys without being converted to a string. Wouldn’t it be nice to be able to do that with other types?

Maps were introduced in ES2015 to solve those problems. Maps only store the key-value pairs you explicitly store in them, and you can use any types you want — including objects! — as keys. Let’s start building some maps.

10.2.1 Creating our first map

We can create an empty map by calling new Map<Key, Value>(), where <Key, Value> is a type parameter that tells TypeScript what kinds of keys and values we’ll be storing in the map. Here’s an example:

Listing 10.11 — Creating a mapTypeScript
interface Ninja {
  name: string;
}
interface NinjaMetadata {
  homeIsland: string;
}

const ninja1 = { name: "Yoshi" };
const ninja2 = { name: "Hattori" };
const ninja3 = { name: "Kuma" };

const ninjaMetadataMap = new Map<Ninja, NinjaMetadata>();  // #A
ninjaMetadataMap.set(ninja1, { homeIsland: "Honshu" });    // #B
ninjaMetadataMap.set(ninja2, { homeIsland: "Hokkaido" });  // #B
console.assert(                                            // #C
  ninjaMetadataMap.get(ninja1)?.homeIsland === "Honshu" &&   // #C
    ninjaMetadataMap.get(ninja2)?.homeIsland === "Hokkaido", // #C
  "The first two ninjas have metadata",                // #C
);                                                       // #C
console.assert(                                            // #D
  ninjaMetadataMap.get(ninja3) === undefined,                // #D
  "There is no mapping for the third ninja",            // #D
);                                                       // #D
console.assert(                                            // #E
  ninjaMetadataMap.size === 2,                            // #E
  "We've created two mappings",                          // #E
);                                                       // #E

ninjaMetadataMap.delete(ninja1);                            // #F
console.assert(                                            // #G
  !ninjaMetadataMap.has(ninja1) &&                          // #G
    ninjaMetadataMap.size === 1,                            // #G
  "There's no first ninja mapping anymore!",             // #G
);                                                       // #G

ninjaMetadataMap.clear();                                 // #H
console.assert(
  ninjaMetadataMap.size === 0,
  "All mappings have been cleared",
);
#A Creates an empty map for mapping ninjas to metadata
#B Maps the first two ninjas to metadata
#C Confirms the mappings for the first two ninja objects using the get method
#D When no mapping exists, get returns undefined
#E The size property tells us how many mappings exist
#F Deletes the mapping for the first ninja
#G The has method tells us whether a mapping exists
#H Uses the clear method to delete all mappings

In listing 10.11, we take advantage of the fact that maps can use objects as keys to store external metadata associated with our ninja objects. Of course, we could store the extra metadata directly on the original objects, but there are cases where we might not want to do that. For example, our code might receive an object argument in a function call that we don’t want to modify because our implicit API contract says that it’s immutable. (We’ll discuss mutability more later in this chapter.) Or we might want to create the metadata for temporary use, then dispose of it when we’re done. Map’s clear() method makes that disposal very easy: all values that aren’t referenced elsewhere will be marked for garbage collection.

It’s important to understand that when we use an object as a map key, it really is the object itself that’s used as the key. Modify the object, and it’ll still work as the same key:

The key is the object, not its contentsJavaScript
ninja1.name = "Not Yoshi";
console.assert(
  ninjaMetadataMap.get(ninja1)?.homeIsland === "Honshu",
  "No matter what his name is, ninja1 is still from Honshu"
);

And conversely, an identical-looking object won’t work as the same key:

A clone is not the same keyJavaScript
const ninja1Clone = { ...ninja1 };
console.assert(
  ninjaMetadataMap.has(ninja1Clone) === false,
  "A clone is no substitute for the real ninja1"
);

Of course, a different variable that references the same object will work just fine:

Same reference, same keyJavaScript
const anotherNinja1 = ninja1;
console.assert(
  ninjaMetadataMap.has(anotherNinja1) === true,
  "The reference matters, not the variable"
);

Put simply, two variables are equivalent as map keys if (and only if) key1 === key2. That goes for primitives as well as objects: it’s perfectly valid for map.get(1) and map.get("1") to have two different values, because 1 !== "1".

10.2.2 Iterating over maps

So far, you’ve seen some of the advantages of maps: you can be sure they contain only items that you put in them, and you can use anything as a key. But there’s more! Because maps are collections, there’s nothing stopping us from iterating over them with for...of loops. You’re also guaranteed that these values will be visited in the order in which they were inserted. Let’s look at the following example.

Listing 10.12 shows three different for...of loops over the same map. The first loop iterates over every mapping, which is returned as a tuple; that is, an array with two items. Through the magic of array destructuring, we immediately assign the items from that tuple to separate key and value variables.

Listing 10.12 — Iterating over a mapTypeScript
const directory = new Map<string, string>();          // #A
directory.set("Yoshi", "+81 26 6462 9152");            // #B
directory.set("Kuma", "+81 52 2378 6462");             // #B
directory.set("Hiro", "+81 76 2771 4624");             // #B

for (const [key, value] of directory) {                  // #C
  console.assert(key !== null, "Key:" + key);                  // #C
  console.assert(value !== null, "Value:" + value);              // #C
}                                                        // #C

for (const key of directory.keys()) {                    // #D
  console.assert(key !== null, "Key:" + key);                  // #D
  console.assert(                                     // #D
    directory.get(key) != null,                            // #D
    "Value:" + directory.get(key),                        // #D
  );                                                  // #D
}                                                     // #D

for (const value of directory.values()) {               // #E
  console.assert(value !== null, "Value:" + value);              // #E
}                                                       // #E
#A Creates an empty string-to-string map
#B Adds three mappings
#C Iterates over each key-value pair in the map
#D Iterates over just the keys in the map
#E Iterates over just the values in the map

Entries, maps, and objects

The [key, value] tuples that we get when we iterate over a map are also known as entries, a term that’s used in some static methods on Object: Object.entries(object), for converting an object to an array of entries, and Object.fromEntries(entries), for converting an iterator that yields entries into an object.

That means that we can use Object.fromEntries(map) to convert a map to an object, with the caveat that the keys have to be converted to strings (which means they may conflict!). More usefully, we can convert an object to a map by converting it to an array of entries and passing that array to the Map constructor: new Map(Object.entries(object)).

The other two loops use the map’s keys and values methods, which return iterator objects. (We learned about iterators in chapter 8.) When we want to iterate over just the keys or just the values from a map, these methods are both handy and efficient. Because they create an iterator object, not an array, they won’t waste memory when iterating over a large map.

Speaking of memory, let’s look at a variant of Map that’s specially designed to avoid memory leaks: WeakMap.

10.2.3 Weakly holding references with WeakMap

JavaScript is a garbage-collected language, which means that it automatically cleans up data from memory when that data is no longer referenced. For the most part, garbage collection is a very nice convenience for developers. But in complex applications, it can be easy to wind up with references to data that we don’t need any more, causing memory leaks.

For example, consider the ninja metadata system from listing 10.11. Imagine if we started using that map to store metadata for ninjas throughout our application:

Metadata for ninjas that come and goTypeScript
const saveNinjaHomeIsland = (ninja: Ninja, homeIsland: string) => {
  ninjaMetadataMap.set(ninja, { homeIsland });
};

Now imagine that those ninjas come and go: different parts of our application create ninjas and save metadata for them, and then discard those ninjas, removing their references to those ninjas. Except — oops! — those ninjas are still used as keys in our metadata map. As a result, neither the ninja objects themselves nor the associated metadata objects will be garbage-collected.

The solution to this problem: WeakMap. The WeakMap type is similar to Map, but it only holds weak references to its keys. If the only references to an object are weak references, that object is eligible for garbage-collection. If a key gets garbage-collected, that entire key-value pair will be removed from the WeakMap.

Storing key-value pairs in a WeakMap is a great way to avoid a common source of memory leaks, but it comes with some caveats compared to Map:

  • WeakMap can only use objects as keys, not primitives.
  • WeakMap doesn’t provide a size property.
  • There’s no way to iterate over a WeakMap.

That last limitation is a big one. Every other collection type we’ve encountered so far is iterable, but with WeakMap, the only way to access its contents is by directly calling get(key). You can’t even convert it to another collection type.

Now you’ve seen the advantages that maps offer over ordinary objects. Let’s move on to a completely different collection type: sets.

10.3 Sets

In many real-world problems, we have to deal with collections of distinct items (meaning each item can’t appear more than once) called sets. You could imagine using a map to track distinct items:

Tracking uniqueness with a mapTypeScript
const items = new Map<unknown, string>();
items.set(1, "an unimportant value");
console.assert(items.has(1) === true);
console.assert(items.has(2) === false);

Sets are a more convenient and efficient alternative to this pattern. You can think of a set as a map with only keys, no values.

10.3.1 Creating our first set

The cornerstone of creating sets is the newly introduced constructor function, conveniently named Set. Let’s look at an example.

Listing 10.13 — Creating a setJavaScript
const ninjas = new Set([                            // #A
  "Kuma",                                          // #A
  "Hattori",                                       // #A
  "Yagyu",                                         // #A
  "Hattori",                                       // #A
]);                                                // #A
console.assert(                                     // #B
  ninjas.has("Hattori"),                            // #B
  "Hattori is in our set",                         // #B
);                                                // #B
console.assert(                                     // #C
  ninjas.size === 3,                               // #C
  "There are only three ninjas in our set!",          // #C
);                                                // #C
ninjas.add("Yoshi");                             // #D
console.assert(ninjas.has("Yoshi"), "Yoshi is added");  // #D
console.assert(
  ninjas.size === 4,
  "There are four ninjas in our set!",
);
console.assert(ninjas.has("Kuma"), "Kuma is already added");
ninjas.add("Kuma");
console.assert(
  ninjas.size === 4,
  "Adding Kuma again has no effect",
);

for (let ninja of ninjas) {                       // #E
  console.assert(ninja !== null, ninja);               // #E
}                                                  // #E
#A Creates a set containing the elements from an array
#B Uses the has method to determine if an element is in the set
#C Uses the size property to determine the size of the set
#D Adds a new item using add
#E Iterates through the set with a for...of loop

In this example we initialized our set using an array of four items. Because two of those items are identical (the string "Hattori"), the duplicate is ignored and the resulting set has three items.

You may notice that there are quite a few similarities to the Map API! The has method and size property are identical. But instead of set(key, value), we have add(item). Likewise, the constructor takes an array of items instead of an array of entries, and the iterator yields items instead of entries.

Adding an existing item to a set is a no-op, just as adding an existing key-value pair to a map is.

Note If you’re calling array.includes(item) repeatedly for the same array, that’s a strong indicator that you should be using a set instead! set.has(item) is a much faster lookup: O(1) instead of O(n).

Let’s go beyond the simple “does this collection have this item?” use case to see some of the more interesting things we can do with sets.

10.3.2 Combining and comparing sets

ES2024 added a variety of methods for set operations, including:

  1. setA.union(setB) for creating a new set with all items that are in either setA or setB
  2. setA.intersection(setB) for creating a new set with all items that are in both setA and setB
  3. setA.difference(setB) for creating a new set with all items that are in setA but not setB
  4. setA.isSubsetOf(setB) for determining whether all of setA’s items are in setB

Let’s look at an example of using intersection to find all warriors who are both a ninja and a samurai:

Intersecting two setsJavaScript
const ninjas = new Set(["Kuma", "Hattori", "Yagyu"]);
const samurai = new Set(["Hattori", "Oda", "Tomoe"]);
const ninjaSamurais = ninjas.intersection(samurai);
console.assert(
  ninjaSamurais.size === 1,
  "There's only one ninja samurai",
);
console.assert(
  ninjaSamurais.has("Hattori"),
  "Hattori is his name",
);

These methods are new enough to be little-used in JavaScript code as of this writing, but if you’re targeting a runtime that supports them (such as Node.js 22 or newer), taking advantage of them will make your code both more readable and more efficient. For an exhaustive list of set methods, see MDN.

10.3.3 Weakly holding references with WeakSet

With all of the similarities we’ve seen between Map and Set, it may not surprise you to learn that Set also has its own weak sibling, WeakSet.

Let’s say that you want to keep track of which ninjas have completed their training. With WeakSet, we can store that information while allowing the ninjas in the set to be garbage-collected:

Tracking graduates with a WeakSetTypeScript
const trainedNinjas = new WeakSet<Ninja>();
const recordNinjaGraduation = (ninja: Ninja) => {
  trainedNinjas.add(ninja);
};

const hasNinjaGraduated = (ninja: Ninja) =>
  trainedNinjas.has(ninja);

WeakSet is a useful tool for avoiding memory leaks, but it has similar caveats to WeakMap:

  • WeakSet can only store objects, not primitives.
  • WeakSet has no size property.
  • You can’t iterate over a WeakSet.

That concludes our coverage of sets. Now let’s move past the discussion of specific collection types and discuss an eternal source of controversy in the JavaScript world: mutability.

10.4 Mutable and immutable collections

All of the collection types we’ve seen so far (objects, arrays, maps, and sets) are mutable collections. That means that their contents can be modified directly (“mutated”). Often, though, mutating a collection is an anti-pattern. In particular, when you pass a collection to an API, there’s a general assumption that you won’t modify that collection after you pass it, and likewise that the API code won’t modify your collection.

Immutable collections, by contrast, are set in stone. That means you never have to worry about them being modified unexpectedly. The tradeoff is that if you want to add or remove an item from an immutable collection, you can’t — you have to create a whole new collection with that change. That can be inefficient (creating a duplicate collection generally requires more CPU and memory than modifying a collection in-place), and it can also require an annoying amount of code.

Let’s look at the reasons why you might need your collections to be immutable. Then we’ll look at some options for achieving that while minimizing the downsides.

10.4.1 The perils of mutability

A common situation that calls for immutability in modern JavaScript is React state. If you’re writing a to-do list component, it might be tempting to write code like this:

Don’t mutate React stateJavaScript
const [todos, setTodos] = useState([]);            // #A
const addTodo = (newTodo) => {
  todos.push(newTodo);                                // #B
}
#A Creates React state with an empty array as the initial value
#B Don’t do this!

In that example, we mutated the todos array with the push method. But that won’t work as intended. The proper way to update the state is to call the state setter with a new array instead:

Create a new array insteadJavaScript
const [todos, setTodos] = useState([]); // initial state is []
const addTodo = (newTodo) => {
  setTodos([...todos, newTodo]); // new array
}

Spreading todos into a new array is an immutable operation, creating a new extended array without modifying the original. This has two important advantages:

  1. When you call the setTodos function, React knows it’s receiving new state, which allows it to re-render the component. If you modified the existing state directly, React would have no idea. (In principle React could wrap the state in a Proxy, as we saw in chapter 9, but wrapping all state in Proxy would add performance overhead.)
  2. When React receives the new state, it still has access to the old state, which it might need. For instance, in concurrency mode it might render the component in batches. The component state needs to remain consistent until it finishes that process.

So how do you make a collection immutable? One option is to use a library that provides immutable collection types, such as Immutable.js. Instead of a native JavaScript array, you’d use Immutable.js’ List type, which provides a convenient read-only interface. Using non-native collection types adds some performance overhead, though, and you’ll likely have to add extra code to to and from native collections as you interface with external APIs.

Another option is to use a mutable collection, then simply avoid mutating it. Of course, that won’t work if you’re worried about the collection being mutated by a third-party library that you pass the collection to! But if you’re only concerned with mutations within your own code, you can prevent that with tooling. You could use an ESLint plugin like eslint-plugin-functional. But there’s a simpler way to prevent mutations in modern JavaScript code: TypeScript’s read-only types.

10.4.2 Read-only collections in TypeScript

TypeScript allows you to declare various collections as read-only, adding compile-time guards against mutation. Here’s an example:

Listing 10.14 — Creating read-only collections in TypeScriptTypeScript
const ninjas = ["Kuma", "Hattori", "Yagyu"] as const;  // #A
ninjas.push("Waluigi"); // TypeScript error              // #B

type NinjaName = (typeof ninjas)[number];                     // #C

interface NinjaMetadata {
  homeIsland: string;
}
const ninjaMetadata: ReadonlyMap<NinjaName, NinjaMetadata> =  // #D
  new Map(                                            // #D
    Object.entries({                                  // #D
      Kuma: { homeIsland: "Honshu" },                    // #D
      Hattori: { homeIsland: "Hokkaido" },                // #D
    }) as [NinjaName, NinjaMetadata][],                     // #D
  );                                                       // #D

ninjaMetadata.set("Yagyu", {                            // #E
  homeIsland: "Figi"                                    // #E
}); // TypeScript error                                // #E
#A Declares an array literal as read-only using as const
#B TypeScript reports an attempt to mutate a read-only array as an error
#C Creates a type from the array: "Kuma" | "Hattori" | "Yagyu"
#D Declares a read-only map initialized from object entries
#E TypeScript reports an attempt to mutate a read-only map as an error

TypeScript’s as const (not to be confused with JavaScript’s const keyword) is a valuable tool: it tells TypeScript to preserve the exact contents of an object or array literal as type information. Normally, our ninjas array’s inferred type would be Array<string>. With as const, it becomes readonly ["Kuma", "Hattori", "Yagyu"], providing more precise type information while also telling TypeScript that this collection should never be modified.

Because of that readonly modifier on the array, TypeScript will error if we call a destructive method like push, or if we try to assign a value to an array item (ninjas[1] = "A replacement"). As with all TypeScript errors, it’s worth emphasizing that this is a compile-time error, not a runtime error. In the compiled JavaScript, ninjas is just a normal, mutable array. And if you pass ninjas to a function that comes from external code, TypeScript has no way of detecting what might happen to it! (If that external code is written in TypeScript, it can use a readonly type for the function argument to indicate that it won’t mutate the argument value.)

The precise type information we preserved with as const allows us to derive a type from the array items: the NinjaName type is defined as encompassing all of the items from the ninjas array, which means it’s equivalent to the string union "Kuma" | "Hattori" | "Yagyu". This is a very handy technique when you want to create a type that matches the items in an array! Similarly, you can create a string union type from the keys of an object with keyof typeof someObject, but only if someObject is defined with as const.

The as const modifier only works for object and array literals, so for maps we have to assign the map to a variable with the type ReadonlyMap. Here we run into some of TypeScript’s limitations: we have to specify the types of the keys and values with type parameters; TypeScript won’t infer them automatically. We also have to use a type assertion to tell TypeScript that the Object.entries result corresponds to our desired map type, because Object.entries flattens our string union type into the simple string type. (Alternatively, we could settle for the less precise ReadonlyMap<string, NinjaMetadata> type, removing the need for the type assertion.)

As with read-only arrays, read-only maps are true JavaScript maps, but with compile-time checks that prevent us from mutating them in our code. As you might guess, TypeScript also provides an analogous ReadonlySet type.

Note that having a read-only type doesn’t prevent a variable from being reassigned. You can still assign a completely new value to that variable, provided that the new value is read-only as well:

Read-only types can still be reassignedTypeScript
let readOnlyArray: ReadonlyArray<number> = [1, 2];
readOnlyArray = [3, 4];                            // #A

const mutableArray = [4, 5];
readonlyArray = mutableArray; // TypeScript error            // #B
#A Assigning a new literal to a read-only type is allowed
#B Assigning a mutable value to a read-only type is not allowed, because the value could be mutated through other references

Using read-only types consistently where appropriate in your TypeScript application will help you avoid common errors involving unintended mutation.

Let’s wrap up our discussion of immutable collections by looking at a solution for one of the common pain points of immutability: how do we perform complex operations on state without directly modifying that state?

10.4.3 Immutable transformations with Immer

When you want to create a new object or array by extending an existing one, that’s easy to achieve with the spread operator:

Extending with the spread operatorJavaScript
const newObject = {...oldObject, newKey: newValue };
const newArray = [ ...oldArray, newItem];

And through the magic of destructuring, it’s easy enough to remove select entries, too:

Omitting with destructuringJavaScript
const {                                       // #A
  omittedKey: _unusedVariable,                     // #A
  ...newObject                                 // #A
} = oldObject;                                 // #A

const [                                       // #B
  _unusedItem,                                 // #B
  ...newArray                                  // #B
] = oldArray;                                  // #B
#A Copies everything but omittedKey to a new object
#B Copies everything but the first array item to a new array

Note Using destructuring to omit values requires assigning those values to unused variables, which may trigger typescript-eslint’s no-unused-vars rule. Fortunately, that rule can be configured to ignore variables whose name match a specified pattern. A common convention is to ignore variables prefixed with _. For more information on the rule’s options, see no-unused-vars.

But what if you’re doing something more complicated? Suppose you have a nested collection that you’re using as state in a framework like React. You want to represent a state change where you:

  1. Update a field on the state object
  2. Add an item to a nested array
  3. Replace an item in a nested map

And you want to do all of that while treating the state object as immutable. That can be challenging to do!

An easy mistake to make would be to copy the state object with const stateCopy = { ...state }, then perform your modifications. That wouldn’t work as intended because the copy would be shallow: any nested objects are just references to the same objects that were attached to the original. For instance, calling stateCopy.array.push(newItem) would modify both stateCopy.array and state.array, because they’re the same array.

Alternatively, you could use a library to make a deep copy before making your changes, but that’s overkill: copying every nested object from the state object, not just the ones you’re modifying, is unnecessary. For a deeply nested object, the process of deep copying could get very expensive in terms of both CPU and memory.

Fortunately there’s an elegant solution to this problem: a library called Immer. Immer allows you to modify immutable collections as if they were mutable. Under the hood, it automatically performs the required copy operations to give you a new copy of that collection with your modifications.

To use Immer, install the immer package. We’ll be using v10 for our example:

$ npm install immer@10

With Immer installed, it’s time for some magic:

Listing 10.15 — Applying mutations to an immutable object with ImmerTypeScript
import { enableMapSet, produce } from "immer";
enableMapSet();                                        // #A

interface NinjaMetadata {
  homeIsland: string;
}
type NinjaState = Readonly<{                           // #B
  ninjas: ReadonlyArray<string>;                      // #B
  ninjaMetadata: ReadonlyMap<string, NinjaMetadata>;   // #B
  lastModified: number;                               // #B
}>;                                                    // #B

const initialState: NinjaState = {                        // #C
  ninjas: ["Kuma", "Hattori", "Yagyu"],                // #C
  ninjaMetadata: new Map(                           // #C
    Object.entries({                                 // #C
      Kuma: { homeIsland: "Honshu" },                   // #C
      Hattori: { homeIsland: "Hokkaido" },               // #C
    }),                                             // #C
  ),                                                // #C
  lastModified: Date.now(),                            // #C
};                                                   // #C

const getStateWithNewNinja = (
  previousState: NinjaState,
  newNinja: string,
  newNinjaMetadata: NinjaMetadata,
): NinjaState => {
  return produce(previousState, (state) => {           // #D
    state.ninjas.push(newNinja);                         // #D
    state.ninjaMetadata.set(newNinja, newNinjaMetadata);  // #D
    state.lastModified = Date.now();                      // #D
  });                                                    // #D
};

const nextState = getStateWithNewNinja(                   // #E
  initialState,                                          // #E
  "Yoshi",                                                // #E
  { homeIsland: "Yoshi's Island" },                        // #E
);                                                       // #E
console.assert(
  nextState.ninjas.length ===
    initialState.ninjas.length + 1,
  "Added a new ninja",
);
console.assert(
  nextState.ninjaMetadata.size ===
    initialState.ninjaMetadata.size + 1,
  "Added metadata for the new ninja",
);
#A Activates an Immer plugin for working with maps and sets
#B Declares a type where all fields and nested collections are read-only
#C Assigns an object to the read-only type, making it effectively immutable
#D Uses Immer’s produce function to make a modified copy of an immutable object
#E Creates a modified copy of our initial state object

Here we have a complex read-only state object that we want to make a modified copy of. At first glance, Immer’s produce function may seem to break the rules: we defined our NinjaState type in a way that prohibits any modification of it, and yet that’s exactly what we appear to be doing in the produce callback! The trick Immer pulls here is that the state argument it gives to the callback isn’t the real state object — though it looks and acts like one. Immer calls this object a draft, in the sense of a work in progress.

Under the hood, the draft is a Proxy, allowing Immer to intercept all of your interactions with it. (We learned about Proxy in chapter 9.) After the produce callback returns, Immer uses those interactions to construct a copy of your original state with those changes applied.

If you look at the TypeScript type for the state draft, you’ll see that it’s a modified version of the NinjaState type that allows mutations. If you were to accidentally try to modify initialState from inside of the produce callback instead of state, the type checker would notice and raise an error.

Immer does come with some caveats: by default, it can only handle objects and arrays; any other collection types require a plugin. (In our example, we called enableMapSet() to activate the built-in maps and sets plugin.) Also, its use of Proxy adds some performance overhead. Immer will always be slower than performing the equivalent copy-and-modify operations directly, which can matter if you’re doing those operations frequently.

With all of that said, Immer is a clever solution to a common problem, and a testament to the flexibility of the JavaScript language!

10.5 Summary

What to remember

  1. Arrays in JavaScript are dynamic and resize automatically when new items are added.
  2. We can modify the contents of an array using several methods accessible from array objects:
    • The built-in push and pop methods add items to and remove items from the end of the array.
    • The built-in shift and unshift methods add items to and remove items from the beginning of the array.
    • The built-in splice method can be used to remove items from and add items to arbitrary array positions.
  3. Arrays have several useful methods:
    • The map method creates a new array with the results of calling a callback on every element.
    • The every and some methods determine whether all or some array items satisfy a certain criterion.
    • The find and filter methods find array items that satisfy a certain condition.
    • The sort method sorts an array in-place.
    • The reduce method aggregates all items in an array into a single value.
  4. Maps are collections of key-value pairs. Whereas objects can only use strings and symbols as keys, maps can use anything as a key.
  5. Sets are collections of distinct items. They’re effectively maps with only keys, no values.
  6. Mutability refers to the ability to modify (“mutate”) a collection. Immutable collections are often preferred to avoid bugs from unexpected mutations.
    • Objects, arrays, maps, and sets are all mutable, but you can make them effectively immutable using TypeScript’s read-only types.
    • Immer allows you to create a modified copy of an immutable collection by applying your changes to a “draft,” which works like a mutable version of that collection.
